---
title: "The Pass Rush: Moves, Stunts, and Why Pressure Beats Sacks"
subtitle: "Four men, about two and a half seconds, and a 315-pound obstacle each: how a defense gets to the quarterback without blitzing, and how to see it from the couch"
description: "The pass rush from the defense's side: get-off and the rush arc; the main moves (speed rush, bull rush, long arm, swim, rip, spin) and the counters built on them (speed-to-power, cross-chop, ghost); the rush plan that sets one move up with another; stunts and games (T-E, E-T, the interior twist) and what they do to slide and man protection; rush lanes, contain and the mush rush against a quarterback who runs; and the numbers: why pressure is steadier than sacks, how much of a sack belongs to the quarterback, pass rush win rate, get-off and time to pressure."
glossary:
  Get-off: "A pass rusher's first movement at the snap: how quickly he reacts to the ball moving and gets across the line of scrimmage. Tracking data measures it in tenths of a second, and a tenth of a second is most of a yard."
  "Speed rush": "A pass rush that tries to beat the offensive tackle around the outside, to the corner of the pocket, before he can get in front: a fast get-off, a curved path (the arc), a dip of the shoulder under the tackle's hands, and a bend back toward the quarterback."
  "Bull rush": "A pass rush straight through the blocker: hands inside on his chest, legs driving, pushing him backward into the quarterback instead of trying to get around him."
  "Long arm": "A power rush move: the rusher locks one arm straight into the blocker's chest, so the blocker cannot reach him, and drives him back, keeping the other hand free to shed the block and escape."
  "Swim move": "A pass rush move that clears the blocker's hands with one hand and then throws the other arm over the top of his shoulder, like a swimming stroke, to get past him."
  "Rip move": "A pass rush move in which the rusher drives his inside arm up under the blocker's arm and through his armpit, like an uppercut, to lift the blocker's arm away and get his own hips past him; the usual finish of a speed rush."
  "Spin move": "A pass rush counter in which the rusher, with the blocker committed to one side, plants and spins all the way around, back toward the other side, to come free; very effective when it works, and it can carry him out of the play when it doesn't."
  "Speed-to-power": "A rush that starts as a speed rush to make the tackle retreat fast, then turns straight into him and converts that speed into a bull rush while his weight is still going backward and he cannot anchor."
  "Cross-chop": "A hand move against a blocker's punch: the rusher swings his outside arm across his own body and chops down on the blocker's hands or forearms, usually followed by a rip or dip, so the blocker never gets a grip."
  "Ghost (rush move)": "A speed move with no hand contact at all, timed to the blocker's punch: at the instant the tackle strikes, the rusher turns his inside shoulder away (and dips it), so the punch hits air and the tackle lunges forward, then bends around him."
  "Rush plan": "A pass rusher's planned sequence of moves across a game: show one move until the blocker adjusts to stop it, then use the counter his adjustment opens."
  Stunt: {def: "A planned pass-rush movement in which two or more rushers exchange gaps after the snap: one goes first to occupy blockers (the penetrator) and the other loops around behind him into the space he left (the looper).", aliases: ["Pass-rush game"]}
  "T-E stunt": "A two-man stunt in which the defensive tackle goes first, driving into the offensive tackle's inside half to pick him and take over contain, and the end loops around behind him into the inside gap the tackle left."
  "E-T stunt": "A two-man stunt in which the end goes first, crashing inside, and the defensive tackle loops around behind him to the outside, taking over the end's rush lane."
  "Rush lane": "The path to the quarterback that each rusher in a four-man rush is responsible for; if every rusher stays in his lane, the quarterback has no gap to step up or escape through, and if one leaves his lane, a hole opens."
  "Mush rush": "A deliberately controlled pass rush, used mostly against quarterbacks who run: the ends give up trying to beat their tackles around the corner and instead push them straight back from their outside shoulders, so the pocket is squeezed from all sides rather than raced into. Also called a cage rush."
  "Pass rush win rate": {def: "ESPN's measure, built from NFL Next Gen Stats tracking data, of how often a pass rusher beats his block within 2.5 seconds of the snap; the fixed clock keeps the quarterback's habits out of the number.", aliases: ["PRWR"]}
---

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (shared drawing helpers for this chapter)"
#| output: false
import logging
logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
import os
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, Polygon, RegularPolygon
from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, style
import gridiron.play as _gp

# Slightly smaller player markers than the book default: this chapter lives in the space between linemen.
_gp.draw_marker.__defaults__ = (None, 0.62)

GREEN = "#0f7a55"          # darker step of the aqua highlight, for text on the light field
PURPLE = style.SERIES[6]   # a ring colour that is neither offense blue nor defense orange
RED = style.SERIES[7]
ARM = style.DEFENSE_DARK
OL_KEYS = ["LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"]
SPLIT = 1.6                # center-to-guard and guard-to-tackle spacing, as in the rest of the book


def O(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label or key)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def line(keys=OL_KEYS):
    """Offensive linemen, labelled so the reader can follow each one."""
    return [O(k, k, -0.7, (OL_KEYS.index(k) - 2) * SPLIT, k) for k in keys]


def four_down(lbs=False):
    """A generic four-man rush: a wide end on each side, a 1-technique shaded on the center's left,
    a 3-technique on the right guard's outside shoulder; optionally two linebackers."""
    out = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -5.4, "E"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "1"),
           D("DT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "3"), D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4, "E")]
    if lbs:
        out += [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, 1.3, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, -2.2, "W")]
    return out


def to(p, key, end, kind="block", via=(), delay=0.0, speed=None):
    """Move `key` through absolute (d, w) points `via` to `end` as a block, rush, path or run."""
    start = np.array(p._cur(key))
    pts = [tuple(np.array(q) - start) for q in (*via, end)]
    if kind == "block":
        return p.block(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "rush":
        return p.rush(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    return {"path": p.path, "run": p.run}[kind](key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)


def timed(p, key, way, kind="path"):
    """Script a player for the frame strips: `way` = [(t, d, w), ...] absolute spots reached at time t
    (seconds after the snap). Standing still between two times is allowed."""
    cur = np.array(p._cur(key), dtype=float)
    tc, wait = 0.0, 0.0
    for t, d, w in way:
        nxt = np.array([d, w], dtype=float)
        dist = float(np.hypot(*(nxt - cur)))
        if dist < 1e-3:
            wait += t - tc
        else:
            p._add(kind, key, [tuple(cur), tuple(nxt)], speed=dist / (t - tc), delay=wait)
            wait = 0.0
            cur = nxt
        tc = t
    return p


def _P(fld, p, d, w):
    return fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.0, ha="center", weight="normal"):
    """A short on-field label at (d, w)."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=12, fontweight=weight,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.92))


def point_to(fld, p, text_at, target, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.8, shrink=7):
    """A label with a thin leader line to the player or spot it names."""
    (xt, yt), (xp, yp) = _P(fld, p, *text_at), _P(fld, p, *target)
    fld.ax.annotate(text, (float(xp), float(yp)), xytext=(float(xt), float(yt)), fontsize=fontsize,
                    color=color, ha="center", va="center", zorder=12,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=color, lw=0.7, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=shrink),
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.92))


def dashed(fld, p, pts, color=RED, lw=1.8, end="arrow", dash=(0, (3, 1.8)), z=6):
    """A dashed path through absolute (d, w) points, ending in an arrow or a block bar ('tee')."""
    xs, ys = _P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    xs, ys = np.asarray(xs, float), np.asarray(ys, float)
    fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=color, lw=lw, ls=dash, zorder=z)
    if end == "arrow":
        fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2] + 0.6 * (xs[-1] - xs[-2]), ys[-2] + 0.6 * (ys[-1] - ys[-2])),
                                         (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=11, color=color,
                                         lw=lw, zorder=z))
    elif end == "tee":
        v = np.array([xs[-1] - xs[-2], ys[-1] - ys[-2]])
        n = np.linalg.norm(v)
        perp = np.array([-v[1], v[0]]) / n * 0.75
        fld.ax.plot([xs[-1] - perp[0], xs[-1] + perp[0]], [ys[-1] - perp[1], ys[-1] + perp[1]], color=color,
                    lw=lw + 0.6, zorder=z)


def pushed(fld, p, a, b):
    """A blocker driven backward from a to b: dashed dark blue with a block bar."""
    dashed(fld, p, [a, b], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.6, end="tee", dash=(0, (2.2, 1.6)), z=4.5)


def arm(fld, p, a, b, lw=3.4, color=ARM):
    """An arm (or hands) as a thick stroke from a to b, with a dot for the hand: dark orange for the rusher,
    dark blue (color=style.OFFENSE_DARK) for the blocker."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, *a), _P(fld, p, *b)
    fld.ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=color, lw=lw, solid_capstyle="round", zorder=9.5)
    fld.ax.plot([x1], [y1], marker="o", ms=4.2, color=color, mec="white", mew=0.6, zorder=9.6)


def curl(fld, p, a, b, rad=-0.6, color=ARM, lw=1.6):
    """A curved arrow from a to b: a hand or arm move (swim over the top, rip up through)."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, *a), _P(fld, p, *b)
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(x0), float(y0)), (float(x1), float(y1)), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                     mutation_scale=10, color=color, lw=lw, zorder=9.5,
                                     connectionstyle=f"arc3,rad={rad}"))


def ghost(fld, p, d, w, label="", side="def", alpha=0.45):
    """A faint marker: where a player is at a moment the static diagram does not otherwise show."""
    x, y = (float(v) for v in _P(fld, p, d, w))
    if side == "def":
        fld.ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=0.62 * 1.25, orientation=np.pi / 4, fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT,
                                        ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.1, alpha=alpha, zorder=7, ls=(0, (2, 1))))
    else:
        fld.ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), 0.62, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="white", lw=0.6, alpha=alpha, zorder=7))
    if label:
        fld.ax.text(x, y, label, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.5, color=style.INK, alpha=0.8, zorder=7.5,
                    fontweight="bold")


def badge(fld, p, d, w, text, color=PURPLE, fontsize=7.4):
    """A small numbered badge on a path: the order in which rushers go."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(float(x), float(y), text, fontsize=fontsize, color="white", ha="center", va="center", zorder=13,
                fontweight="bold", bbox=dict(boxstyle="circle,pad=0.18", fc=color, ec="white", lw=0.6))


def lane(fld, p, pts, color=style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.11):
    """Shade a rush lane: a polygon through absolute (d, w) points."""
    xy = np.array([_P(fld, p, d, w) for d, w in pts], dtype=float)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Polygon(xy, closed=True, fc=color, alpha=alpha, ec=color, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1.4))


def clean(ax):
    """Box-zoomed diagrams: drop hash ticks and yard numbers, clip text to the window."""
    for ln in list(ax.lines):
        xs, ys = ln.get_data()
        if len(xs) == 2 and ln.get_linewidth() == 0.5 and np.hypot(xs[1] - xs[0], ys[1] - ys[0]) < 1.0:
            ln.remove()
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()
        else:
            t.set_clip_on(True)


def draw(p, width_in=5.8, ax=None, ol_fs=None, **kw):
    """Play.draw, sized for the page and cleaned for a box-sized window. ol_fs shrinks the two-letter line
    labels (LT, LG, RG, RT) on wide figures, where the default size overprints."""
    fld = p.draw(width_in=width_in, ax=ax, **kw)
    clean(fld.ax)
    if ol_fs:
        for t in fld.ax.texts:
            if t.get_text() in ("LT", "LG", "RG", "RT"):
                t.set_fontsize(ol_fs)
    return fld


def panel_title(ax, text, size=8.4):
    ax.set_title(text, loc="left", fontsize=size, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)


def note_below(ax, text, size=6.8):
    ax.text(0.5, -0.02, text, transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=size, color=style.INK,
            linespacing=1.2)


def pdf_build():
    return os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")


# --- frame strips (print) and video (web) for the simulated plays ---------------------------
MARK_R = 0.6
RING_R = 0.9


def tracking(play):
    df = play.to_tracking()
    df["_id"] = df["displayName"].astype(str)
    return df


def panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings=(), links=()):
    """One moment of a simulated play: markers, faint trails, rings, and 'who has whom' links."""
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
    ylo, yhi = sorted((play.ball_y - lateral[0], play.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=play.los, window=window, numbers=False, hashes=False,
                lateral=(ylo, yhi), to_go=play.to_go)
    cur = df[df["frameId"] == fid]
    shown = cur[cur["x"].between(play.los + window[0] + 0.5, play.los + window[1] - 0.5)
                & cur["y"].between(ylo + 0.5, yhi - 0.5) & (cur["side"] != "ball")]
    ids = set(shown["_id"])
    trails = df[(df["frameId"] <= fid) & df["_id"].isin(ids)]
    for (_, side), g in trails.groupby(["_id", "side"]):
        xs, ys = fld.xy(g["x"].values, g["y"].values)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.4, zorder=3)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for _, r in shown.iterrows():
        x, y = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(r["x"], r["y"]))
        lab = str(r.get("label", "") or "")
        if r["side"] == "off":
            ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), MARK_R, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=8))
            tc = "white"
        else:
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=MARK_R * 1.3, orientation=np.pi / 4,
                                        fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=8))
            tc = style.INK
        fs = max(4.0, min(7.5, ppy * (0.8 if len(lab) <= 1 else 0.55)))
        ax.text(x, y, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=tc, fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
    for key, col in rings:
        r = cur[cur["displayName"] == key].iloc[0]
        x, y = fld.xy(r["x"], r["y"])
        ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), RING_R, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.7, zorder=7))
    for a, b, col in links:
        pa = cur[cur["displayName"] == a].iloc[0]
        pb = cur[cur["displayName"] == b].iloc[0]
        xs, ys = fld.xy(np.array([pa["x"], pb["x"]]), np.array([pa["y"], pb["y"]]))
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=col, lw=1.5, ls=(0, (1, 1.4)), zorder=9)
    return fld


def strip(play, times, notes=None, lateral=(-9, 9), window=(-9, 6), ncols=3, rings=(), width_in=6.5,
          final_links=()):
    """Numbered, captioned frame strip with a fixed box-sized window, so markers stay legible in print."""
    df = tracking(play)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(times) / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, squeeze=False,
                             figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * span_d / span_w + (0.6 if notes else 0.25))))
    for ax in axes.flat[len(times):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times)):
        panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings, final_links if i == len(times) - 1 else ())
        ax.set_title(f"{i + 1}.  " + ("snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.1f} s"),
                     fontsize=8.2, color=style.INK_2, loc="left")
        if notes:
            note_below(ax, notes[i], size=6.9)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.0 if notes else 0.5, w_pad=0.5)
    return fig


def video(play, times, notes=None, lateral=(-9, 9), window=(-9, 6), rings=(), width_in=5.4):
    """Web version of the strip: every frame, with the strip's notes as running captions."""
    import shutil
    from matplotlib import animation
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    df = tracking(play)
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width_in, width_in * span_d / span_w + 0.4))
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()

    def update(fid):
        ax.clear()
        t = float(tmap[fid])
        panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings)
        txt = "snap" if abs(t) < 0.05 else f"{t:+.1f} s"
        if notes:
            cur = [n.replace("\n", " ") for tt, n in zip(times, notes) if tt <= t + 1e-6]
            txt += ("   " + cur[-1]) if cur else ""
        ax.set_title(txt, fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK, loc="left")
        return []

    frames = [f for f in sorted(df["frameId"].unique()) if float(tmap[f]) >= -0.3]
    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=frames, interval=100)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def rush_animation(play, times, notes=None, **kw):
    """Video on the website; a numbered, captioned frame strip in the PDF."""
    if pdf_build():
        strip(play, times, notes=notes, **kw)
        plt.show()
    else:
        video(play, times, notes=notes, **{k: v for k, v in kw.items() if k in ("lateral", "window", "rings")})
```

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (the data behind this chapter's numbers: nflverse via nflreadpy)"
#| output: false
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

SEAS = list(range(2018, 2026))
_part = nfl().load_participation(seasons=SEAS).to_pandas()[
    ["nflverse_game_id", "play_id", "was_pressure", "number_of_pass_rushers"]]
_plays = pbp(SEAS, columns=["game_id", "play_id", "season", "season_type", "week", "qtr", "posteam", "defteam",
                            "qb_dropback", "sack", "passer_id", "passer", "epa", "pass_attempt", "complete_pass",
                            "sack_player_name", "time"])
ALL = _plays[_plays["qb_dropback"] == 1].merge(_part, left_on=["game_id", "play_id"],
                                               right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "play_id"], how="left")
# Pressure includes sacks. (In the NGS seasons, 2018-2022, the flag is blank on sacks; FTN, 2023-2025, fills it.)
ALL["press"] = ALL["was_pressure"].astype(float).fillna(0).gt(0) | ALL["sack"].eq(1)
DB = ALL[ALL["season_type"] == "REG"].copy()

# Defensive team-seasons
TS = DB.groupby(["season", "defteam"]).agg(db=("sack", "size"), sacks=("sack", "sum"), sr=("sack", "mean"),
                                           pr=("press", "mean")).reset_index()
TS["p2s"] = TS["sr"] / TS["pr"]
FTN = TS[TS["season"] >= 2023].copy()
R_FTN = np.corrcoef(FTN["pr"], FTN["sr"])[0, 1]
P2S_FTN = DB.loc[(DB["season"] >= 2023) & DB["press"], "sack"].mean()
PR_FTN = DB.loc[DB["season"] >= 2023, "press"].mean()
SR_FTN = DB.loc[DB["season"] >= 2023, "sack"].mean()


def ts(team, season):
    return FTN[(FTN["defteam"] == team) & (FTN["season"] == season)].iloc[0]


CLE24, CLE25, DEN25, SF25 = ts("CLE", 2024), ts("CLE", 2025), ts("DEN", 2025), ts("SF", 2025)
TOP_PR = FTN.sort_values("pr").iloc[-1]

# Year-to-year carry-over, within one charting source only (no 2022 -> 2023 pair: the source changes)
PAIRS = [s for s in SEAS[:-1] if s != 2022]


def carry(frame, key, a_col, b_col=None, min_n=None):
    b_col = b_col or a_col
    out = []
    for s in PAIRS:
        a = frame[frame["season"] == s].set_index(key)
        b = frame[frame["season"] == s + 1].set_index(key)
        if min_n is not None:
            a, b = a[a["n"] >= min_n], b[b["n"] >= min_n]
        j = a[[a_col]].join(b[[b_col]], rsuffix="_next", how="inner").dropna()
        out.append(j.iloc[:, 0].corr(j.iloc[:, 1]))
    return np.array(out)


QS = DB[DB["press"]].groupby(["season", "passer_id"]).agg(n=("sack", "size"), p2s=("sack", "mean"),
                                                          name=("passer", "first")).reset_index()
CARRY = {
    "Defense: pressure rate": carry(TS, "defteam", "pr"),
    "Defense: sack rate": carry(TS, "defteam", "sr"),
    "Defense: pressure rate\n(predicting next year's sack rate)": carry(TS, "defteam", "pr", "sr"),
    "Defense: pressure-to-sack rate": carry(TS, "defteam", "p2s"),
    "Quarterback: pressure-to-sack rate": carry(QS, "passer_id", "p2s", min_n=100),
}
MEAN = {k: float(np.mean(v)) for k, v in CARRY.items()}
K_PR, K_SR, K_X, K_DP, K_QP = (MEAN[k] for k in CARRY)

# Super Bowls LIX and LX: the winners' rush, from FTN's charting of the games
def sb(game, team):
    g = ALL[(ALL["game_id"] == game) & (ALL["defteam"] == team)]
    return dict(db=len(g), four=int((g["number_of_pass_rushers"] <= 4).sum()),
                press=int(g["press"].sum()), press4=int((g["press"] & (g["number_of_pass_rushers"] <= 4)).sum()),
                sacks=int(g["sack"].sum()), sacks4=int(((g["sack"] == 1) & (g["number_of_pass_rushers"] <= 4)).sum()))


LIX, LX = sb("2024_22_KC_PHI", "PHI"), sb("2025_22_SEA_NE", "SEA")

# What a pressure costs even without a sack: EPA per dropback, FTN seasons
F3 = DB[DB["season"] >= 2023]
EPA_CLEAN = F3.loc[~F3["press"], "epa"].mean()
EPA_PNS = F3.loc[F3["press"] & (F3["sack"] == 0), "epa"].mean()
EPA_SACK = F3.loc[F3["sack"] == 1, "epa"].mean()
_att = F3[F3["pass_attempt"] == 1]
CMP_CLEAN = _att.loc[~_att["press"], "complete_pass"].mean()
CMP_PNS = _att.loc[_att["press"] & (_att["sack"] == 0), "complete_pass"].mean()

# The quarterback's share: (1) the spread of pressure-to-sack rates, 2023-2025 pooled, QBs with 200+ pressured
# dropbacks; (2) FTN's charters' own call on whose fault each sack was (is_qb_fault_sack)
QP = F3[F3["press"]].groupby("passer_id").agg(n=("sack", "size"), p2s=("sack", "mean"), name=("passer", "first"))
QP = QP[QP["n"] >= 200].sort_values("p2s")
Q_LO, Q_HI, Q_N = QP.iloc[0], QP.iloc[-1], len(QP)
FULL = {"B.Nix": "Bo Nix", "W.Levis": "Will Levis", "S.Howell": "Sam Howell", "J.Love": "Jordan Love"}
Q_LO_NAME, Q_HI_NAME = FULL.get(Q_LO["name"], Q_LO["name"]), FULL.get(Q_HI["name"], Q_HI["name"])
Q_25, Q_75 = QP["p2s"].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
FTNC = nfl().load_ftn_charting(seasons=[2023, 2024, 2025]).to_pandas()[
    ["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id", "is_qb_fault_sack", "n_blitzers", "n_pass_rushers"]]
_sk = F3[F3["sack"] == 1].merge(FTNC, left_on=["game_id", "play_id"],
                                right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id"], how="left")
QB_FAULT = _sk["is_qb_fault_sack"].astype(float).mean()

# Seattle's four-man rushes in Super Bowl LX: how many included a blitzer (a simulated pressure), per FTN
_lx = ALL[(ALL["game_id"] == "2025_22_SEA_NE") & (ALL["defteam"] == "SEA")].merge(
    FTNC, left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id"], how="left")
_lx4 = _lx[_lx["n_pass_rushers"] == 4]
LX_FOUR_FTN, LX_SIM = len(_lx4), int((_lx4["n_blitzers"] > 0).sum())

# Garrett's record-breaking sack (Week 18, 2025, at Cincinnati: from play-by-play)
_g = ALL[(ALL["season"] == 2025) & (ALL["week"] == 18) & (ALL["defteam"] == "CLE") & (ALL["sack"] == 1)
         & ALL["sack_player_name"].eq("M.Garrett")].iloc[0]
G_QTR, G_CLOCK, G_QB = int(_g["qtr"]), str(_g["time"]).lstrip("0"), str(_g["passer"])

# How many rushers? FTN charting, 2023-2025 regular seasons
_nr = DB.loc[(DB["season"] >= 2023) & DB["number_of_pass_rushers"].notna(), "number_of_pass_rushers"]
FOUR_SHARE, FIVE_PLUS = (_nr == 4).mean(), (_nr >= 5).mean()
```

Third-and-8, early in the second quarter. The offense spreads four receivers and keeps the back in to
block; the defense shows four linemen and nobody else near the line. At the snap the right defensive end
takes three long strides up the outside, and the offensive tackle in front of him kick-slides back fast to
stay between him and the quarterback. Then, with the tackle's weight going backward, the end plants his
outside foot and drives straight into the tackle's chest. The tackle's feet stop moving; he is walked
backward three yards, into the spot where the quarterback wanted to set his feet. The quarterback throws a
beat early, off his back foot, and the pass sails over a receiver who was about to come open. Incomplete.
Punt. The box score records nothing for the end: no sack, no tackle, not even a hit. His position coach
will grade it as one of his best plays of the day. This chapter is about why.

**You'll be able to:**

- Name the main pass-rush moves (speed, bull, long arm, swim, rip, spin) as you see them, and say which
  mistake by the blocker each one punishes.
- Explain how a rusher *plans* his moves across a game, and spot the counter when a tackle starts guessing.
- Recognise a stunt (T-E, E-T, interior twist) from the crossing paths, and say what it was trying to do to
  the protection.
- Read rush lanes and contain, and explain why defenses "mush rush" a quarterback who can run, and what that
  costs them.
- Explain why pressure is a steadier measure of a pass rush than sacks, and how much of a sack belongs to the
  quarterback.
- Use pass rush win rate, get-off and time to pressure, and know what each can and cannot tell you.

- **[Pass Protection](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd)**: the [pocket](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pocket)
  is a cup (the interior holds, the tackles give ground); [slide](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slide-protection)
  protection blocks gaps and [man](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-protection) protection blocks men; the
  tackle's [kick slide](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-kick-slide) and [vertical set](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-vertical-set),
  the blocker's [punch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-punch) and [anchor](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-anchor);
  linemen [passing off](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pass-off-switch-vs-stay) a stunt; and the numbers:
  [pressure](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pressure), [pressure rate](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pressure-rate),
  [time to throw](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-time-to-throw). This chapter is the same fight from the other side.
- **[Defensive Line Play](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd)**:
  technique numbers from the defense's side (the **3-technique** on the guard's outside shoulder, the **1** shaded on
  the center, the 5 and the [wide-9](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wide-9) outside the tackle),
  [one-gap](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-one-gap) penetration, and [contain](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-contain):

**How to read the diagrams.** Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares, and *left* and *right* are the
offense's. The linemen are LT, LG, C, RG and RT; Q is the quarterback (usually drawn at his
[launch point](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-launch-point), the spot he throws from) and R the running back. On
defense, E is an [edge rusher](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-edge-rusher): a 4-3 defensive end with his hand down or
a 3-4 outside linebacker standing up, since the rush is the same job. The defensive tackles are labelled by technique
(**1**, **3**), and the drills use the coverage labels from Part 06 (CB, NB, FS, SS, M and W for the linebackers). An
orange arrow is a rusher's path; a blue line ending in a short bar is a blocker's set. The few other marks are
explained with the first figure that uses them.

## The rusher's problem: a race and a fight

The quarterback in today's NFL releases the ball a little under three seconds after the snap on average
([Pass Protection](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd) has the numbers), and on a quick throw in
well under two. An edge rusher who lines up outside the tackle has to cover an arc of about thirteen yards to reach
the spot where the quarterback sets his feet; a defensive tackle in the middle has nine or so, straight ahead, but
through the thickest traffic on the field. Unblocked, an edge rusher would cover his arc in roughly two seconds. He
is never unblocked. A man who weighs about 315 pounds, who knows where the quarterback will be and only has to stay
in the way, is standing on the path.

So a pass rush is two contests at once. It is a **race**: the rusher has to get to the quarterback before the ball
leaves, and a rusher who arrives at 3.4 seconds against a quarterback who threw at 2.6 has done nothing, however
good his move was. And it is a **fight**: to win the race he has to beat a blocker who is bigger, who has the inside
position, and who is allowed to use his hands too. The rusher's advantages are the two the blocker lacks. He knows
the snap is coming and where he is going, and he moves *forward*, while the blocker moves backward.

There is a third fact, and it explains why defenses pay pass rushers so much: **most of the time, the defense rushes
only four.** In FTN's charting of the 2023–2025 regular seasons, `{python} f"{100 * FOUR_SHARE:.0f}%"` of dropbacks
faced exactly four rushers and `{python} f"{100 * FIVE_PLUS:.0f}%"` faced five or more.[^rushers] A
[blitz](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) can manufacture a free rusher by sending
more men than the offense can block, but every extra rusher is one fewer defender in coverage, and the quarterback
knows it. Four rushers against five or six blockers leaves seven defenders to cover at most five receivers. If those
four can create pressure by themselves, the defense gets to the quarterback *and* covers everybody. That is the
holy grail of defensive football, and this chapter is about how it is done: by moves, by plans, and by stunts.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
A four-man rush is the balance point between coverage, which is expensive, and pressure, which is valuable. A team
whose four can win their fights gets pressure without paying for it in coverage, which is why an edge rusher who wins
them is usually the highest-paid player on his defense.
:::

## Get-off: the first step decides more than you think

The fight begins before anyone touches anyone. A rusher's [**get-off**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-get-off)
is his first movement at the snap: how quickly he reacts to the ball moving and gets across the line of scrimmage.

Defenders are not allowed to move into the neutral zone before the snap, and unlike the offense they do not know the
snap count. So a rusher does not listen to the quarterback's cadence; he watches the ball, or the center's hand on it,
and goes the instant it moves. The offense's weapons against this are a varied snap count (a "hard count" to draw a
rusher offside, a quick count to catch him flat-footed) and, in a loud stadium, a silent count, which takes away the
hard count but can leave the snap on a rhythm (the center looks back, the guard taps him, the ball comes on a set beat)
that a good rusher learns to time.
The rusher's weapon is a stance with his weight already tilted forward and a first step that covers ground without
popping up.

Why does a tenth of a second matter so much? Because of what it does to the meeting point.

```{python}
#| label: fig-get-off
#| fig-cap: "Two edge rushers on the same arc against the same tackle, 1.2 seconds after the snap (the faint squares are where each rusher is at that moment; the line is the path both run; the faint circle is the tackle, who has kick-slid back to his set point). The rusher who moved the instant the ball did has already reached the tackle's depth, his hips level with the tackle's: the tackle has to open up and run with him, and is in trouble. The rusher who started three-tenths of a second later is still a couple of yards upfield of the tackle, where the tackle can meet him square and punch. Same speed, same path; the only difference is the first step."
p = Play(line(["RG", "RT"]) + [O("QB", "QB", -7.2, 0.0, "Q")], [D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4, "E")], los=35, to_go=None)
ARC = [(1.0, 5.4), (-0.6, 6.3), (-2.8, 6.0), (-4.4, 4.8), (-6.2, 1.6)]
to(p, "RE", ARC[-1], "rush", via=ARC[1:-1])
to(p, "RT", (-2.5, 4.4))
fld = draw(p, width_in=5.4, lateral=(-2.2, 10.8), window=(-9.4, 3.2))


def along(pts, s):
    """The point a distance s (yards) along a polyline."""
    for a, b in zip(pts[:-1], pts[1:]):
        seg = float(np.hypot(b[0] - a[0], b[1] - a[1]))
        if s <= seg:
            f = s / seg
            return (a[0] + f * (b[0] - a[0]), a[1] + f * (b[1] - a[1]))
        s -= seg
    return pts[-1]


def run_dist(t, t0, acc=8.0, vmax=7.5):
    """Yards covered by time t for a rusher who starts at t0, accelerates at acc to vmax."""
    dt = max(0.0, t - t0)
    t_top = vmax / acc
    return 0.5 * acc * dt ** 2 if dt <= t_top else 0.5 * acc * t_top ** 2 + vmax * (dt - t_top)


FAST, SLOW = along(ARC, run_dist(1.2, 0.10)), along(ARC, run_dist(1.2, 0.40))
GAP_YD = run_dist(1.2, 0.10) - run_dist(1.2, 0.40)
ghost(fld, p, *FAST, "E")
ghost(fld, p, *SLOW, "E")
ghost(fld, p, -2.5, 4.4, side="off", alpha=0.35)
point_to(fld, p, (-4.6, 8.9), FAST, "fast get-off at 1.2 s:\nlevel with the tackle,\nturning the corner",
         color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, shrink=9)
point_to(fld, p, (0.9, 8.9), SLOW, "0.3 s slower:\nstill upfield of him", color=style.INK_2, shrink=9)
point_to(fld, p, (-5.6, 3.9), (-2.5, 4.4), "the tackle's set\nat 1.2 s", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, shrink=8)
say(fld, p, -7.6, 3.6, "flatten to the QB", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

At full speed an edge rusher covers about seven yards a second, so a tenth of a second at the snap is most of a yard
on the arc. In @fig-get-off the two rushers differ by three-tenths, and by 1.2 seconds that has become a
`{python} f"{GAP_YD:.1f}"`-yard difference in where they meet the tackle. The quick one meets him *level*, at the
tackle's own depth, where the tackle has to turn his hips to run with him, and a blocker who turns his hips has given
up the inside and lost most of his power. The slow one meets him *in front*, where the tackle is square, balanced and
ready to punch. Same athlete, same path, a completely different fight.

That is why scouts time rushers' first steps at the Combine (the league's pre-draft testing event), why defensive
line coaches drill get-off every day, and why the best rushers are often the first player on the field to move.
Tracking data now measures it directly: Next Gen Stats times how long a rusher takes to cross the line of scrimmage
after the snap and quotes it in its broadcasts and analysis.[^getoff] For a scale: the quickest single snaps it has
highlighted are around a third of a second, best-ever reps. A lineman whose body starts about a yard behind the ball
needs roughly half a second to cross it from a standstill, so most rushes take longer; the simulated rushers at the end
of this chapter take half a second to eight-tenths.

## The arc and the corner

Before the moves, the geometry they are all trying to bend. An edge rusher's basic path is the **arc**: a curve up
the outside of the tackle and around him toward the quarterback. He aims it at a **landmark**, not at the blocker: the
quarterback's launch point, about seven or eight yards behind the line from the shotgun, which is why the diagrams put
Q there. The tackle's answer, as Pass Protection showed, is to
kick-slide back and out, staying between the rusher and that spot, and to push the rusher *past* the quarterback if he
keeps running. The pocket is a cup, and a rusher run around the rim of the cup ends up behind it, harmless.

How wide the rusher lines up is the first trade. A wide alignment like the
[wide-9](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wide-9) gives him a running start and room to build speed, at the cost of a
longer arc and a soft spot inside him that draws and screens are built to punish; a tight alignment over the tackle
gives him a shorter path and power, but no space to work.

The rusher wins the arc at one spot: the **corner**, the moment his hips draw level with the tackle's. Before that, the
tackle is in front of him and can punch and steer. Once the rusher's hips are past, the tackle is beside or behind him,
can only push, and any push sends the rusher where he wanted to go. (His last resort is to grab: a hold, ten yards if
the official sees it.) That is why the last part of every good edge rush is a tight turn back toward the quarterback,
**flattening** the arc once he is past the tackle rather than continuing upfield.

Two physical skills decide whether a rusher can do this, and you can see both on any broadcast replay. The first is
**bend**: the ability to lean his whole body toward the inside, ankles flexed, shoulder almost at the turf, while
running at full speed, so he can turn the corner tightly instead of drifting wide. The second is **dip**: dropping the
shoulder nearest the tackle so the tackle's reaching hands slide off it. Watch a great edge rusher win and you will see
a body tilted at an angle that looks like it should fall over.

One coaching rule sits under all of it: **rush half a man**. A rusher never attacks the blocker's whole chest, where
the blocker is strongest; he attacks one half of him, a shoulder, so the blocker has to turn to stay in front. Every
move below starts on a shoulder.

The tackle, of course, knows all this. If he gets deep enough fast enough, there is no corner to turn. He can also get
it wrong in the other direction and **overset**: retreat wider or deeper than the rush in front of him needs, opening
his hips to the outside too early, which leaves the space inside him empty. And so the rusher needs other ways to win:
through the tackle, or back inside him. That is what the moves are.

## The moves

There are dozens of named pass-rush moves, and every rusher has his own blend, but almost all of them belong to a
handful of families. Six are worth knowing by sight. In each panel of @fig-rush-moves the rusher (E) lines up outside
the right tackle; read the note under each panel for what the move attacks.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rush-moves
#| fig-cap: "Six pass-rush moves against a right tackle (zoomed in on him; the quarterback is off the bottom-left of each panel, where the rush arrows are heading). The orange arrows show where the rusher goes; the arm work is in the note under each panel. New marks: a dashed dark-blue line ending in a bar is the blocker being driven backward, and a faint circle is where he ends up; a thick dark-orange stroke ending in a dot is the rusher's arm; a curved orange arrow is a hand move. Bull rush: chest to chest, walking him backward. Long arm: the same push from arm's length, with a dashed escape route once the tackle is driven back. Swim: sell outside, arm over the top, go inside. Rip: an uppercut through his outside arm to get the hips past. Spin: when he has overcommitted to the outside, spin back inside. Each move beats a different mistake."
LAT_M, WIN_M = (-0.6, 8.6), (-6.4, 2.6)
MOVES = [
    ("1  Speed rush", (-2.6, 4.5), [(-0.5, 6.5), (-2.4, 6.4), (-3.6, 5.3)], (-5.2, 3.0),
     "Win the race to the corner, dip\nunder his hands, bend back.\nBeats a slow or short set.", "dip\nand bend"),
    ("2  Bull rush", (-1.6, 3.8), [(-0.8, 4.5)], (-3.3, 3.4),
     "Hands inside, chest to chest,\nwalk him into the QB. Beats a\nhigh set or one already bailing.", "drive\nthrough him"),
    ("3  Long arm", (-1.9, 3.9), [(-0.8, 4.9)], (-2.6, 4.6),
     "One arm locked out: he can't\nreach you. Drive him back,\nthen shed and go.", "arm\nlocked out"),
    ("4  Swim", (-2.2, 4.8), [(0.2, 6.2), (-1.0, 4.5), (-2.2, 3.0)], (-4.8, 1.6),
     "Jab outside, clear his hands,\narm over the top, inside.\nBeats a tackle who bites outside.", "over\nthe top"),
    ("5  Rip", (-2.4, 4.4), [(-0.6, 6.3), (-2.2, 5.8), (-3.4, 4.8)], (-5.1, 2.6),
     "Uppercut up through his outside\narm and shoulder, hips past.\nThe finish of most speed rushes.", "rip\nthrough"),
    ("6  Spin", (-2.7, 5.3), None, (-5.0, 2.0),
     "He oversets for the arc: plant,\nspin all the way round, inside.\nBig reward, big risk.", "spin\ninside"),
]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(6.6, 6.3))
for ax, (name, rt_end, via, end, note, tag) in zip(axes.flat, MOVES):
    p = Play(line(["RG", "RT"]), [D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4, "E")], los=35, to_go=None)
    to(p, "RT", rt_end)
    if via is None:   # the spin: up the arc, a full turn, then back inside
        c, rr = np.array([-2.45, 5.85]), 0.5
        th0 = np.arctan2(6.35 - c[1], -2.0 - c[0])
        loop = [tuple(c + rr * np.array([np.cos(a), np.sin(a)])) for a in np.linspace(th0, th0 + 2 * np.pi, 14)]
        via = [(-0.6, 6.4), (-2.0, 6.35)] + loop[1:] + [(-3.2, 3.9)]
    to(p, "RE", end, "rush", via=via)
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, title=False, lateral=LAT_M, window=WIN_M)
    if name.endswith("Bull rush"):
        pushed(fld, p, (-1.6, 3.8), (-4.3, 2.9))
        ghost(fld, p, -4.3, 2.9, side="off")
    elif name.endswith("Long arm"):
        pushed(fld, p, (-1.9, 3.9), (-3.7, 3.6))
        ghost(fld, p, -3.7, 3.6, side="off")
        arm(fld, p, (-2.6, 4.6), (-3.25, 4.0))
        dashed(fld, p, [(-2.6, 4.6), (-3.4, 5.25), (-4.3, 5.0), (-4.9, 3.9)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.6)
    elif name.endswith("Swim"):
        curl(fld, p, (-0.4, 5.7), (-1.9, 3.7), rad=0.8)
    elif name.endswith("Rip"):
        curl(fld, p, (-1.8, 5.9), (-3.0, 4.6), rad=-0.7)
    say(fld, p, *((-0.9, 7.3) if name.endswith("Long arm") else (-4.9, 6.2)), tag, color=ARM, weight="bold",
        fontsize=6.6)
    panel_title(ax, name)
    note_below(ax, note)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.6, w_pad=0.7)
plt.show()
```

**The speed rush.** The [**speed rush**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-speed-rush) is the move everything else is
built on: beat the tackle to the corner before he can get in front. Fast get-off, a curved path up the arc, a dip of
the near shoulder as the tackle reaches for him, and a bend back toward the quarterback. It beats a tackle who sets too
slowly or not deep enough, and it is the move tackles fear most, which is exactly why it makes every other move work:
a tackle who is worried about speed retreats fast, and a man retreating fast is off balance in other ways. Its
weakness is the one the pocket is built around: a
tackle who gets deep enough simply runs the rusher past the quarterback.

**The bull rush.** The [**bull rush**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bull-rush) is the opposite idea. Instead of
going around the blocker, the rusher goes *through* him: hands inside on the chest, hips low, legs churning, driving
him straight back into the quarterback. A bull rush rarely produces a sack by itself; what it produces is a collapsing
pocket. A quarterback who has a tackle or guard backing into his feet cannot step up, cannot finish his throwing motion
and often cannot see. It beats a blocker who sets too high (pads up, so the rusher gets under him) or one whose weight
is already going backward because he retreated too fast, since a man moving backward cannot plant and push. The
blocker's answer is the
[anchor](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-anchor): sink the hips, widen the base, and stop the slide. A bull rush
against a blocker who anchors is a stalemate, and a stalemate is a win for the offense.

**The long arm.** The [**long arm**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-long-arm) is the bull rush with an escape hatch.
The rusher locks one arm, fully extended, into the blocker's chest (usually his inside arm into the outside half of
the blocker's chest, the near breastplate). Why can the blocker not just reach back? Because a punch is thrown with both
hands and square shoulders, which keeps the elbows bent; one arm locked straight, with the rusher's shoulder turned into
it, reaches several inches farther. So the blocker's hands fall short of the rusher's body, the rusher controls the
distance between them and drives the blocker back with it, and his other hand stays free to knock the blocker's hands
away and slip off the block when the moment comes. It has become one of the signature moves of the
modern NFL edge rusher, because it works for long-armed athletes who are not giant men, and because it lets a rusher
generate power without getting tied up chest to chest.

**The swim.** The [**swim move**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-swim-move) clears the blocker's hands with one hand
and throws the other arm over the top of his shoulder, like a swimmer's overhand stroke, to get past him. On the edge it
is usually an inside move: the rusher fakes outside to make the tackle widen, then swims back inside. In the middle it
is a staple of quick, compact defensive tackles who meet guards almost at once. It needs timing and a blocker whose
weight has gone the wrong way, and its risk is visible in the drawing: for a moment the rusher's arm is up and his chest
is open, and a blocker who is not fooled will drive right into it.

**The rip.** The [**rip move**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rip-move) is an uppercut: the rusher drives his inside
arm up under the blocker's arm and through his armpit, lifting the arm off him and turning his own shoulder through the
gap so his hips get past. It is the usual way a speed rush is *finished*, because at the corner the tackle's outside hand
is the last thing between the rusher and the quarterback, and the rip takes that hand away. A dip and a rip together are
the most common sight on an edge sack.

**The spin.** The [**spin move**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spin-move) is the showpiece. When the tackle has
committed to the outside, the rusher plants his outside foot, turns his back to the blocker and spins all the way round,
coming out back inside him toward the quarterback. Dwight Freeney made it famous with the Colts in the 2000s, and it
carried him to the Hall of Fame.[^freeney] Done at the right moment, against a tackle who has overset, it leaves the
blocker grabbing air. Done at the wrong one, against a blocker who stayed square, it spins the rusher out of the
pocket, and for half a second he cannot even see the quarterback: big reward, big risk.

**Telling them apart on the broadcast.** The speed rush and the rip look like one motion: the rusher's outside shoulder
dips, his inside arm swings up through the tackle's armpit, and he flattens toward the quarterback. In a bull rush the
two men are chest to chest and the tackle's helmet is snapped back; in a long arm there is daylight between them, one
arm locked straight across it, and the tackle's arms flailing short. A swim shows an arm going *over* the tackle's
shoulder, like a freestyle stroke, as the rusher goes inside; a spin shows the rusher's back to the camera for an
instant.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Pass rushers win with strength." Strength helps, especially in the bull rush and the long arm, but most rush wins are
wins of *timing and position*: a quicker first step, hands that land before the blocker's do, a move chosen for the set
the blocker just showed. It is the mirror of Pass Protection's point that most protection losses are losses of
position.
:::

### Moves are counters to hands

Watch a pass rush closely and you will see that the rusher's hands are busy before his feet have done anything clever.
The blocker's main weapon is his [punch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-punch), a two-handed strike into the
rusher's chest to stop his momentum and steer him. Many moves are built specifically to beat that punch.

The two oldest are power moves. The **club** is a forearm or open-hand blow to the blocker's shoulder or elbow that
knocks his punch aside, usually to set up a rip or a swim. The **push-pull** (also called a snatch or a jerk) grabs
the blocker, pulls him forward past the rusher just as he leans in, and lets go: the interior rusher's signature move,
because guards meet rushers almost at once and lean into them.

```{python}
#| label: fig-hands
#| fig-cap: "Two modern hand moves against the tackle's punch, in close-up (the tackle's punch is drawn in dark blue). Cross-chop: as the tackle's hands come out, the rusher swings his outside arm across his own body (curved arrow) and chops them down, then rips past while the tackle's hands are out of position. Ghost: the rusher never touches him. At the instant of the punch he turns his inside shoulder away and dips it (the faint square is where his shoulder was), so the punch lands on air and the tackle lunges forward, off balance, as the rusher bends around him."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.6))
for ax, name in zip(axes, ("1  Cross-chop", "2  Ghost")):
    p = Play(line(["RG", "RT"]), [D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4, "E")], los=35, to_go=None)
    to(p, "RT", (-1.9, 3.9))
    if name.endswith("chop"):
        to(p, "RE", (-4.6, 3.0), "rush", via=[(-0.4, 5.6), (-1.6, 5.2), (-3.0, 4.6)])
    else:
        to(p, "RE", (-4.7, 3.1), "rush", via=[(-0.6, 5.8), (-1.6, 5.6), (-2.9, 5.0)])
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, title=False, lateral=(-0.4, 9.0), window=(-6.4, 4.8))
    if name.endswith("chop"):
        arm(fld, p, (-1.9, 3.9), (-1.25, 4.55), lw=2.6, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
        curl(fld, p, (-0.2, 6.3), (-1.55, 4.15), rad=0.55, lw=1.8)
        say(fld, p, 2.9, 6.0, "outside arm\nchops down", color=ARM, weight="bold", fontsize=6.6)
        point_to(fld, p, (-3.9, 6.9), (-1.3, 4.5), "his punch,\nknocked down", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, shrink=4)
        say(fld, p, -5.2, 5.1, "rip past", color=ARM, fontsize=6.6)
    else:
        ghost(fld, p, -1.15, 4.75)
        arm(fld, p, (-1.9, 3.9), (-1.2, 4.7), lw=2.6, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
        point_to(fld, p, (-3.9, 6.9), (-1.2, 4.7), "his punch\nhits air", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, shrink=4)
        say(fld, p, 2.9, 6.0, "shoulder turned\naway, no contact", color=ARM, weight="bold", fontsize=6.6)
        say(fld, p, -5.2, 5.4, "bend\naround", color=ARM, fontsize=6.6)
    panel_title(ax, name)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()
```

The [**cross-chop**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cross-chop) is the clearest example (@fig-hands). As the tackle
punches, the rusher swings his outside arm across his own body and chops down on the tackle's hands or forearms,
knocking the punch down and away, then rips or dips past while the tackle's hands are out of position. It turns the
blocker's best tool into the reason he loses. On a replay it looks like a karate chop: the rusher's arm sweeps across
his chest and the tackle's arms drop.

The [**ghost (rush move)**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-ghost-rush-move) goes one step further: no hand contact at
all. A dip lowers the shoulder under hands that are already reaching; a ghost is *timed to the punch*. At the instant
the tackle strikes, the rusher turns his inside shoulder away, so the punch lands on nothing and the tackle, having
thrown his weight into a strike that hit air, lunges forward off balance as the rusher bends around him. On a replay,
look for the tackle reaching at empty space, often falling forward. A ghost works best against a tackle who punches
early and hard; a patient tackle who "catches" the rusher and strikes late gives it nothing to avoid, which is one
reason many NFL tackles have stopped throwing one textbook punch at every rusher.

Rules shape this hand fight too. A rusher may use his hands on a blocker's body, but thrusting them up into the blocker's head or neck is a foul
(an illegal use of hands, five yards and an automatic first down when the defense does it).[^hands] That rule has a
history you will meet below, and it is why the modern hand fight is aimed at the blocker's hands, arms and chest.

## The rush plan: setting up the move you want

Here is the real secret of pass rushing, and the reason the moves above are only half the story. A tackle facing the
same rusher thirty-odd times in a game is not guessing blindly; he is studying the rusher too, and he adjusts. So the best
rushers do not just have moves. They have a [**rush plan**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rush-plan): a planned
sequence across the game that shows the blocker one move until he adjusts to stop it, then uses the counter his
adjustment has opened.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rush-plan
#| fig-cap: "Why a rush plan works: every way the tackle sets opens something else (zoomed on the right tackle; the quarterback is off the bottom-left). Left: after being beaten around the edge, he oversets, kicking wide at the snap to take the corner away; the space inside him (shaded) opens, and the rusher counters back inside with a spin or swim. Middle: worried about the inside, he sets short and square; now the corner is open and the speed rush wins it. Right: worried about speed, he bails straight back as fast as he can; his weight is going backward, so when the rusher turns into his chest he cannot plant and anchor, and is driven back (dashed): the speed-to-power. The blocker cannot protect all three at once, so the rusher's job is to make him choose and then punish the choice."
PLAN = [
    ("He oversets: inside opens", (-2.9, 5.5), [(-0.6, 6.4), (-1.7, 6.0), (-2.2, 4.0)], (-5.0, 2.0),
     "Counter: back inside\n(spin or swim)"),
    ("He sets short: corner opens", (-1.3, 3.8), [(-0.6, 6.6), (-2.6, 6.4), (-3.8, 5.2)], (-5.3, 3.0),
     "Counter: speed around\nthe edge"),
    ("He bails: power opens", (-2.6, 4.4), [(-0.6, 6.3), (-1.4, 5.9)], (-1.95, 5.0),
     "Counter: speed-to-power\nthrough his chest"),
]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.6, 3.55))
for ax, (name, rt_end, via, end, note) in zip(axes, PLAN):
    p = Play(line(["RG", "RT"]), [D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4, "E")], los=35, to_go=None)
    to(p, "RT", rt_end)
    to(p, "RE", end, "rush", via=via)
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, title=False, lateral=LAT_M, window=WIN_M)
    if "inside" in name:
        x, y = _P(fld, p, -2.9, 3.0)
        ax.add_patch(Ellipse((float(x), float(y)), 2.2, 2.6, fc=RED, alpha=0.13, ec=RED, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)),
                             zorder=1.5))
        say(fld, p, -4.6, 6.0, "inside is\nopen", color=RED, weight="bold", fontsize=6.6)
    elif "corner" in name:
        x, y = _P(fld, p, -2.6, 6.3)
        ax.add_patch(Ellipse((float(x), float(y)), 2.2, 2.6, fc=RED, alpha=0.13, ec=RED, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)),
                             zorder=1.5))
        say(fld, p, -4.6, 1.6, "corner is\nopen", color=RED, weight="bold", fontsize=6.6)
    else:
        pushed(fld, p, (-2.6, 4.4), (-4.6, 3.7))
        ghost(fld, p, -4.6, 3.7, side="off")
        point_to(fld, p, (-5.3, 6.6), (-2.6, 4.4), "weight going\nback: no anchor", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
                 fontsize=6.4)
    panel_title(ax, name, size=7.8)
    note_below(ax, note, size=7.0)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

The logic in @fig-rush-plan is a triangle. Speed threatens the corner, so the tackle must get depth, and there are
only two ways to get it fast. Get it by widening, and the inside opens for the spin or swim. Get it by retreating
straight back at full speed, and his weight is going backward, which is exactly when power works. So he must stay
balanced and patient, which slows his set, which brings speed back. A rusher with one great move can be planned for. A
rusher with two that look the same for the first two steps cannot.

That is the job of [**speed-to-power**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-speed-to-power), probably the single most
important move in the modern edge rusher's kit. It starts exactly like a speed rush: the same get-off, the same first
steps up the arc. The tackle, seeing speed, kicks back fast. Then, two or three steps in, the rusher turns straight into
him and converts all that speed into a bull rush, hitting him while his weight is still going backward, when he cannot
anchor. It is the move in this chapter's opening, and it works *because* of the speed rush: the more a tackle fears the
corner, the faster he retreats, and the more his own momentum helps the rusher push him.

You can follow a rush plan from the couch. Early, many rushers show speed again and again, to make the tackle think
about the corner. Once he starts bailing, the counters come: the inside spin, the speed-to-power, the long arm. A
tackle who has been beaten inside starts to sit, and the speed rush is back on. The plan is built during the week from
film of that specific tackle (his set depth, whether he punches early, whether he oversets after being beaten), so the
same rusher may use a completely different plan the following Sunday.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In Madden a pass-rush move is a button press, and whether it works is mostly a matter of ratings. Real moves work or
fail depending on what the blocker is afraid of, which depends on what the rusher showed him on the previous ten snaps.
The spin that beats a tackle in the fourth quarter would have been stuffed in the first, before he had a reason to
overset. Pass rushing is a conversation across a game, not a series of independent dice rolls.
:::

## Inside rushers: less room, shorter path

Everything above is described from the edge, where most sacks are recorded. Defensive tackles play a different
version of the same game. An interior rusher has the shortest path to the quarterback, and pressure up the middle is the most destructive
kind: the quarterback cannot step up into it and cannot see over it. But he also has the least room to work. A guard is
on him almost immediately (there is no long arc to set up a move, only a yard or so of space), and he often faces two
blockers. That is the four-against-five arithmetic from the start of the chapter: five linemen against four rushers
leaves one blocker spare, and the spare is usually the center, who sits in the middle and can turn either way to help
a guard. Interior rushers therefore win with fast, compact hands: a club or a push-pull the instant they meet the
guard, a swim or a rip past him, a bull rush to push the pocket. When the ball is coming out too quickly to get home,
they do the next-best thing and get their hands up into the throwing lane; a batted pass is an interior rusher's
win. And they are measured differently. A 3-technique who drives the guard back into the quarterback's lap, forcing him to slide away from the
pressure and into an edge rusher's arms, may have done more than the edge rusher who gets credited with the sack.

The greatest interior rusher of the modern era made the case that a defensive tackle could be the most important player
on the field. Aaron Donald, a 6-foot-1 defensive tackle the Rams drafted 13th overall in 2014, won Defensive Player of
the Year three times (2017, 2018 and 2020) and had 20.5 sacks in 2018, astonishing for a player who lined up inside and
was double-teamed constantly.[^donald] What made him special was not size. It was get-off, hand speed and leverage:
he was often past the guard before the guard had finished his first step, the one-gap penetration of
[Defensive Line Play](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd) applied to the
pass, and his hands (the club, the push-pull, the swim) were too quick for a double team to land cleanly.

## Stunts: winning with geometry instead of muscle

Moves win one-on-one fights. A [**stunt**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-stunt), also called a
[**pass-rush game**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pass-rush-game) or a twist, wins by making two blockers'
assignments collide. In a stunt, two or more rushers exchange gaps after the snap: one goes first to occupy blockers
(the **penetrator**), and the other loops around behind him into the space he left (the **looper**). The defense still
rushes four, still covers with seven; it just rearranges where the four go.

You saw the most common stunt from the offense's side in Pass Protection,
where the guard and tackle passed it off by switching. Here are the main families from the defense's side.

```{python}
#| label: fig-stunts
#| fig-cap: "Three common stunts, each zoomed on the part of the line it attacks (the defensive linemen are drawn about half a yard deeper than in the book's other diagrams, so the loops have room to show; the badge above each rusher gives the order he goes in). T-E: the 3-technique goes first and drives into the right tackle's inside half, picking him; the guard follows the 3 outside, and the end loops in a tight hook behind the 3's starting spot into the space the guard left. E-T: the mirror. The end crashes inside first and picks the guard, the tackle chases him inside, and the 3-technique loops around to the outside lane the tackle vacated. Interior twist (T-T): the 3-technique crashes through the right guard's inside shoulder into the A gap, picking the guard and the center; the 1-technique wraps over the top behind him into the B gap the 3 left. In each, two blockers end up on one man (or on nobody), and the second rusher arrives where nobody is."
DL_DEEP = 1.6   # depth at which the defensive linemen are drawn (the book default is 1.0), so the loops show
STUNTS = [
    ("T-E stunt", ["RG", "RT"], ["DT", "RE"], (-1.0, 7.0),
     {"DT": ([(0.4, 3.3)], (-0.5, 3.7)),
      "RE": ([(0.9, 5.5), (2.0, 4.6), (2.35, 3.2), (2.0, 1.7), (0.4, 0.9)], (-3.4, 0.7))},
     {"RG": ((-1.4, 2.6), []), "RT": ((-1.7, 4.6), [])}),
    ("E-T stunt", ["RG", "RT"], ["RE", "DT"], (-0.4, 7.6),
     {"RE": ([(0.5, 3.9)], (-0.3, 2.9)),
      "DT": ([(2.2, 2.6), (2.45, 3.9), (2.0, 5.2), (0.3, 5.7)], (-3.1, 4.6))},
     {"RG": ((-1.3, 1.9), []), "RT": ((-1.7, 3.5), [])}),
    ("Interior twist (T-T)", ["LG", "C", "RG", "RT"], ["DT", "NT"], (-3.0, 5.0),
     {"DT": ([(0.5, 1.4)], (-0.4, 0.95)),
      "NT": ([(2.2, -0.3), (2.45, 1.0), (2.3, 2.3), (0.6, 2.7)], (-3.2, 2.1))},
     {"LG": ((-1.5, -1.8), []), "C": ((-1.3, 0.1), []), "RG": ((-1.4, 1.35), []), "RT": ((-1.6, 3.4), [])}),
]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.6, 3.7))
for ax, (name, ol, dl, lat, paths, sets) in zip(axes, STUNTS):
    p = Play(line(ol), [q.moved(d=DL_DEEP) for q in four_down() if q.key in dl], los=35, to_go=None)
    for k in dl:
        via, end = paths[k]
        to(p, k, end, "rush", via=via)
    for k, (end, via) in sets.items():
        to(p, k, end, via=via)
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, title=False, lateral=lat, window=(-5.0, 4.0))
    for n, k in enumerate(dl, 1):
        q = p.players[k]
        badge(fld, p, q.d + 1.35, q.w, str(n))
    panel_title(ax, name, size=8.0)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

**The T-E stunt.** In a [**T-E stunt**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-t-e-stunt) (tackle first, end second) the
defensive tackle drives into the offensive tackle's inside half to pick him, then takes over contain, and the end loops
around behind him into the inside gap he vacated. The penetrator's aiming point is the near hip of the *far* blocker
(the offensive tackle, not the guard in front of him): he has to collide with both blockers, a legal **pick**, so they
cannot switch cleanly. A penetrator who just runs around the tackle has wasted the stunt. If the guard follows the
3-technique outside and the tackle waits for the end on the outside, both block the wrong man, and the end walks
through the gap.

**The E-T stunt.** The [**E-T stunt**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-e-t-stunt) is the mirror: the end crashes
inside first, picking the guard, and the tackle loops around him to the outside, taking over the end's rush lane. It
sends the looper wide, toward an offensive tackle who has just watched the end leave and may have turned inside to
chase him.

**Which one, when?** Both hunt the same seam; the difference is who arrives second, unblocked or against the wrong
man. Defenses usually make the best rusher the looper, so a star end means T-E (he loops inside onto a guard, who is
slower than a tackle and rarely sees an end) and a quick, rangy 3-technique means E-T (he loops outside onto a tackle
who is turned the wrong way). The matchup matters too: aim the looper at the weaker blocker, and the pick at the one
who switches poorly.

**The interior twist.** Two defensive tackles can do the same thing in the middle, a **T-T twist**. In @fig-stunts the
3-technique crashes through the right guard's inside shoulder into the A gap, picking the guard and the center, and the
1-technique wraps over the top behind him into the B gap he left. It attacks the guards and center, the three men who
are supposed to hold firm, and it is especially effective against centers who have to make the protection calls and
then find a man.

The words overlap: many staffs say "stunt" for run-down line movement and "game" or "twist" for a pass-rush exchange,
the penetrator is also the crasher or picker, and the looper the wrapper. Each stunt gets a code word ("Tex" is a common
one for T-E), and many defenses run three-man games too. Most stunts come in the coordinator's call, but many lines
also have games they can check into at the line when they see a particular protection.

### Why stunts work, and what they cost

Stunts exist because they create a mismatch or a free rusher *without blitzing*. Against man protection, the
blockers have to recognise the stunt and pass it off in a split second; if either one hesitates, the looper is free.
Against slide protection, as you are about to see, a stunt aimed the wrong way is simply absorbed, but one aimed at the
right spot can still choose who blocks whom.

The animation shows a T-E against a slide going the other way. Compare it with the stunt figure in
[Pass Protection](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd), where the right tackle *took*
the crashing 3-technique: that line was in man protection and switched. Here the line is sliding, so the tackle steps
inside to his gap and lets the 3-technique go by.

```{python}
#| label: fig-te-vs-slide
#| fig-cap: "A T-E stunt against slide protection (simulated; zoomed on the offense's right side, linebackers and coverage not shown because they drop). The line slides left, toward the 1-technique shaded in the left A gap, so each lineman steps left and owns the gap to his left: the right guard owns the right A gap, the right tackle the B gap, and the back's job is the right end. The 3-technique (ringed in purple) crashes outside, out of the tackle's gap and into the back's area; the end (ringed in green) jabs upfield and loops behind him into the B gap. The slide does its job: the tackle keeps his gap and picks up the looping end, so nobody is free. (The right guard, with nobody in his gap, does what slide rules tell him: he looks the way the slide is going and helps the center on the 1-technique, so he never sees the stunt behind him.) But the stunt has changed the matchup: the back, set to block a 250-pound end, meets a 300-pound defensive tackle at full speed and is driven back toward the quarterback, who has to slide away. Dotted lines in the last frame: who finished on whom."
def te_vs_slide():
    """A four-man rush: T-E stunt on the right against a full slide left, the back assigned to the right end."""
    p = Play(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 1.7, "R")], four_down(), los=35,
             to_go=None)
    timed(p, "QB", [(0.8, -6.8, 0.0), (2.0, -6.8, 0.0), (2.6, -7.0, -0.9)])
    # the slide: everyone steps left; the left side is blocked normally
    timed(p, "LE", [(0.5, -0.4, -5.8), (1.0, -1.8, -5.9), (1.6, -3.0, -5.4), (2.6, -4.6, -4.6)], "rush")
    timed(p, "LT", [(0.5, -1.5, -4.2), (1.0, -2.3, -4.6), (1.6, -3.0, -4.5), (2.6, -4.0, -3.9)], "block")
    timed(p, "LG", [(0.4, -1.2, -2.5), (0.8, -1.6, -2.7), (1.6, -2.0, -2.6), (2.6, -2.4, -2.5)], "block")
    timed(p, "NT", [(0.4, 0.0, -0.9), (0.8, -0.5, -1.0), (1.6, -1.0, -1.0), (2.6, -1.2, -1.0)], "rush")
    timed(p, "C", [(0.4, -1.3, -0.9), (0.8, -1.7, -1.0), (1.6, -2.2, -1.1), (2.6, -2.6, -1.1)], "block")
    timed(p, "RG", [(0.4, -1.3, 0.8), (0.8, -1.7, 0.6), (1.3, -2.1, 0.4), (2.6, -2.7, 0.35)], "block")
    timed(p, "RT", [(0.4, -1.2, 2.4), (0.8, -1.6, 2.15), (1.3, -1.9, 2.2), (1.8, -2.2, 2.3), (2.6, -2.7, 2.3)],
          "block")
    # the penetrator: the 3-technique crashes outside, through the space the RT stepped away from
    timed(p, "DT", [(0.4, 0.1, 3.4), (0.8, -0.8, 4.2), (1.3, -2.0, 4.4), (1.8, -3.1, 3.9), (2.2, -3.9, 3.0),
                    (2.6, -4.6, 2.2)], "rush")
    # the looper: the end jabs upfield, then loops behind the 3-technique into the B gap
    timed(p, "RE", [(0.4, 0.2, 5.6), (0.8, 0.6, 4.6), (1.3, -0.3, 3.2), (1.8, -0.8, 2.6), (2.6, -0.6, 2.7)], "rush")
    # the back steps up to take the end outside the tackle, and meets the 3-technique instead
    timed(p, "RB", [(0.4, -4.6, 2.4), (0.8, -4.1, 3.4), (1.3, -3.6, 4.0), (1.8, -4.5, 3.2), (2.2, -5.4, 2.3),
                    (2.6, -6.5, 1.1)], "block")
    return p


rush_animation(te_vs_slide(), [0.0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.3, 1.8, 2.6],
    notes=["snap: the line slides left;\nR has the right end", "line steps left; 3 crashes\noutside, E jabs upfield",
           "RT lets the 3 go;\nE loops behind him", "RT picks up the E;\nR meets the 3, not the E",
           "a 300-lb tackle\non a 210-lb back", "R driven back, Q slides away:\nnobody free, still pressure"],
    lateral=(-2.6, 8.4), window=(-8.6, 2.6), ncols=3, rings=(("DT", PURPLE), ("RE", style.THIRD)),
    final_links=(("RT", "RE", GREEN), ("RB", "DT", RED)))
```

Notice what the stunt did and did not do in @fig-te-vs-slide. It did not produce a free rusher: the slide protection
handled it exactly as designed, because the right tackle owned a *gap*, not a man, and simply took whoever came into it.
That is slide protection's strength: gaps do not move. What the stunt did instead was **choose the matchup**. The protection had assigned the back to the end. The
stunt swapped the end for a defensive tackle who outweighs the back by ninety pounds, and the back lost. No one was
unblocked, and the quarterback was still pressured.

Run the same T-E into the *slide side*, where the center, guard and tackle are all stepping toward it, and it dies:
the guard owns the B gap the end loops into, the tackle owns the C gap the 3-technique crashes into, and each blocker
simply takes the man who arrives. So defenses aim stunts away from the slide, at the man side of a half-slide, or at a
specific blocker: a slow-footed guard, a rookie tackle, a back who has to take a lineman.

How does the defense know which way the slide will go before the snap? It mostly doesn't *know*; it bets on clues.
Film shows how an offense protects from each formation and each back alignment, so the back's spot is a clue to
the offense's habits. Before the snap the center points out the linebacker he is
counting from, which hints at the slide's direction. And many defenses simply shift or align late, so the slide is
called against a picture that changes. Line coaches talk about
stunts the way offensive coordinators talk about plays, as weapons chosen for a particular opponent.

Stunts have three costs, and they are why defenses do not stunt on every snap.

- **They take time.** The looper runs a longer path than a straight rush, so a stunt usually arrives later, about two
  and a half seconds or more after the snap. Against a quick throw, a stunt is a defense that rushed two men late and
  two men sideways. Stunts belong on long-yardage downs, when the quarterback must hold the ball for routes to develop.
- **They give up the one-on-one.** The penetrator's job is to occupy blockers, not to win, so a great rusher who is
  asked to penetrate on a stunt is a great rusher not rushing. Defenses often build stunts so their best player is the
  looper.
- **They open lanes.** Two rushers crossing paths leave, for a moment, a space where neither of them is, and a
  quarterback who can run will find it. That is the next subject.

## Rush lanes and contain

A four-man rush is not four men running at the quarterback. It is four men each responsible for a **lane**, and the
lanes together form a box around him.

A [**rush lane**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rush-lane) is the path to the quarterback that one rusher owns. The
two ends usually own the outside lanes and have [contain](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-contain): they rush outside
the tackles but must not run past the quarterback's depth, because the space behind them would become a running lane.
The two interior rushers own the middle and have the job of pushing the pocket straight back, so the quarterback cannot
step up. If every rusher stays in his lane, the quarterback has nowhere to go: forward is the interior push, sideways is
the edge rushers, backward is a longer throw. If one rusher leaves his lane, there is a hole.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rush-lanes
#| fig-cap: "Rush lanes (shaded) for a four-man rush, with the quarterback at his launch point. The arrows show each rusher's lane, not the hand fight; in a real rush every one of them is engaged with a blocker along the way. Left: lanes kept. The ends rush outside the tackles and stop at the quarterback's depth (the dashed contain line), the inside rushers push the pocket straight back, and the quarterback is boxed in. Right: one lane lost. The right end, chasing the sack, runs his arc past the quarterback's depth; the right tackle rides him past (that is the tackle's job), and the space they have both left becomes an escape lane (red). A quarterback who can run climbs and slips out underneath them, often past the line of scrimmage before anyone can turn around. A right-handed quarterback escapes to his right most readily, which is why this side's contain matters most."
LANES = {"LE": [(1.0, -5.4), (-1.2, -6.5), (-4.6, -6.1), (-6.7, -2.0)], "NT": [(1.0, -0.7), (-5.0, -0.7)],
         "DT": [(1.0, 2.35), (-5.0, 1.0)], "RE": [(1.0, 5.4), (-1.2, 6.5), (-4.6, 6.1), (-6.7, 2.0)]}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.1))
for ax, lost in zip(axes, (False, True)):
    p = Play(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -7.0, 0.0, "Q")], four_down(), los=35, to_go=None)
    for k, sp in {"LT": (-3.4, -4.3), "LG": (-1.9, -1.8), "C": (-1.6, 0.0), "RG": (-1.9, 1.8), "RT": (-3.4, 4.3)}.items():
        if not (lost and k == "RT"):
            to(p, k, sp)
    if lost:   # the right tackle rides the end past the quarterback
        to(p, "RT", (-6.4, 5.7), via=[(-2.4, 5.0)])
    for k, pts in LANES.items():
        if lost and k == "RE":
            to(p, "RE", (-9.3, 4.4), "rush", via=[(-1.2, 6.5), (-5.0, 6.8), (-8.0, 6.2)])
        else:
            to(p, k, pts[-1], "rush", via=pts[1:-1])
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, title=False, lateral=(-11.6, 11.6), window=(-11.6, 3.0), ol_fs=5.4)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for k, pts in LANES.items():
        xs, ys = _P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.9 * ppy, alpha=0.13 if not (lost and k == "RE") else 0.05,
                solid_capstyle="round", solid_joinstyle="round", zorder=1.4)
    for sgn in (-1, 1):
        (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, -7.0, sgn * 2.6), _P(fld, p, -7.0, sgn * 8.6)
        ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=2)
    if lost:
        dashed(fld, p, [(-7.0, 0.6), (-5.4, 2.4), (-3.0, 4.1), (1.8, 4.2)], color=RED, lw=2.0)
        point_to(fld, p, (-2.4, 9.0), (-2.2, 4.12), "escape\nlane", color=RED, fontsize=7.0)
        say(fld, p, -10.0, 8.2, "too deep", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        point_to(fld, p, (-6.0, 9.0), (-6.4, 5.9), "tackle rides\nhim past", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4)
        panel_title(ax, "One lane lost")
    else:
        say(fld, p, -8.7, -5.6, "contain line:\nnot past the QB", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4)
        say(fld, p, -3.5, 0.15, "push the\npocket", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4)
        panel_title(ax, "Lanes kept: the QB is boxed in")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()
```

The trade in @fig-rush-lanes is the oldest one in pass rushing. A rusher who stays disciplined in his lane gives the
quarterback nowhere to go, but he also gives up some of his own chance to get home. A rusher who abandons his lane for
the sack, whether by running too far upfield, spinning inside out of an outside lane, or looping on a stunt, may get
there, or may open the door. Against a quarterback who will stand in the pocket, the gamble usually pays. Against one
who runs, it often doesn't. Defenses guard the contain on the quarterback's throwing-arm side hardest (the offense's
right, for a right-hander), because he can escape that way and still throw on the run.

Stunts make the lanes move. On a T-E, the penetrator crashing outside takes over the outside lane and with it contain,
while the end who usually has contain loops inside. If the penetrator does not get there, or gets there too deep, the
edge is open. That is part of why stunts are rarer against running quarterbacks, and why the stunts defenses do run
against them are often the ones that keep a fast player outside.

## The mush rush: squeezing instead of racing

Keeping lanes is ordinary discipline: every good four-man rush does it, and every end in it is still trying to beat
his tackle to the corner and then stop at the quarterback's depth. Against a quarterback who is a real threat to run,
defenses often go further and change what the rush is *for*. In a [**mush rush**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mush-rush)
(some staffs say **cage rush**), the ends stop trying to win the corner at all. Each one stays on his tackle's outside
shoulder, in front of him, and pushes him straight back, with a bull rush or a long arm, until the tackle is standing
beside the quarterback. The inside rushers do the same to the guards. The pocket is squeezed from all sides rather
than raced into, and the goal is no longer to sack him quickly. It is to make sure that when the routes are covered and
he looks for somewhere to run, there is nowhere to go.

```{python}
#| label: fig-mush
#| fig-cap: "The mush rush against a quarterback who runs. Nobody goes around anybody: the ends (ringed) stay on the outside shoulders of their tackles and drive them straight back to the quarterback's depth (dashed), and the inside rushers drive the guards back into his face. The cage (green outline) is made of driven-back blockers with rushers on their outside shoulders: it shrinks around him but never opens. Some defenses add a spy, a linebacker who stays at home and mirrors the quarterback side to side (M), as a last line if he does escape."
```
