```{python}
p = Play(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -6.2, 0.0, "Q")], four_down() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 5.0, 0.0, "M")], los=35,
         to_go=None, title="The mush rush: a cage, not a race")
to(p, "C", (-1.6, 0.0))
p.highlight("LE", "RE", color=PURPLE)
fld = draw(p, width_in=5.6, lateral=(-11.5, 11.5), window=(-10.2, 8.4), ol_fs=5.8)
for sg in (-1, 1):
    pushed(fld, p, (-0.7, sg * 3.2), (-5.3, sg * 3.4))      # tackles walked back
    ghost(fld, p, -5.3, sg * 3.4, side="off")
    dashed(fld, p, [(1.0, sg * 5.4), (-0.6, sg * 5.0), (-4.3, sg * 4.6)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.6, dash="solid")
    ghost(fld, p, -4.3, sg * 4.6)                           # end on the tackle's outside shoulder
    pushed(fld, p, (-0.7, sg * 1.6), (-3.0, sg * 1.7))      # guards walked back
    ghost(fld, p, -3.0, sg * 1.7, side="off")
dashed(fld, p, [(1.0, -0.7), (-1.7, -1.4)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.6, dash="solid")
dashed(fld, p, [(1.0, 2.35), (-1.7, 1.9)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.6, dash="solid")
ghost(fld, p, -1.7, -1.4)
ghost(fld, p, -1.7, 1.9)
cage = [(-4.3, -4.6), (-1.7, -1.4), (-1.6, 0.0), (-1.7, 1.9), (-4.3, 4.6), (-6.2, 4.2), (-8.2, 1.6), (-8.6, 0.0),
        (-8.2, -1.6), (-6.2, -4.2)]
xy = np.array([_P(fld, p, d, w) for d, w in cage], dtype=float)
fld.ax.add_patch(Polygon(xy, closed=True, fc=GREEN, alpha=0.10, ec=GREEN, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1.5))
(xa, ya), (xb, yb) = _P(fld, p, 6.3, -2.2), _P(fld, p, 6.3, 2.2)
fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(xa), float(ya)), (float(xb), float(yb)), arrowstyle="<|-|>", mutation_scale=9,
                                 color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.3, zorder=9))
point_to(fld, p, (-6.6, -8.8), (-4.3, -4.6), "ends: on the tackle's\noutside shoulder,\ndrive him back",
         color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
point_to(fld, p, (-6.6, 8.8), (-5.3, 3.4), "tackle walked back\nbeside the QB:\nno escape lane", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
point_to(fld, p, (3.0, -3.6), (-3.0, -1.7), "inside: drive the\nguards into his face", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
say(fld, p, 6.3, 5.4, "spy (optional):\nmirrors the QB", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, -9.0, 4.0, "the cage", color=GREEN, weight="bold")
plt.show()
```

The word "mush" sounds passive, and the mush rush is often criticised as timid when it fails. But watch it work against
a great runner and it is anything but. The rushers are still fighting their blockers; they are fighting them for
*position* rather than for a path around them. The quarterback ends up throwing from a shrinking space with no lanes,
or running into a defender who was waiting for exactly that.

The cost is the clock. A mush rush produces fewer quick pressures and fewer sacks, so the coverage behind it has to
hold for four or five seconds instead of two and a half. Against a quarterback who is both a great runner and a patient
passer, that is a miserable choice, which is why such quarterbacks are so hard to defend. Some defenses add the
[spy](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spy) you met in
[Linebackers](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-04-linebackers-and-second-level.qmd), a defender assigned
only to mirror the quarterback; it buys insurance at the cost of a man in coverage or in the rush.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"A mush rush means the defense isn't trying to get to the quarterback." It means the defense has decided *where* it
wants the quarterback to be, and has accepted that he will get there later. Against a quarterback who runs for a first
down every time a lane opens, a sack is less valuable than an escape is costly.
:::

## Measuring a pass rush: why pressure beats sacks

A [sack](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd), the quarterback tackled behind the line
before he can throw, is the pass rush's famous statistic, and for good reason: it is one of the most damaging plays in
football. It costs yards, a down and often the drive, and sometimes the ball. The NFL has counted sacks officially only
since 1982;[^sacks82] the single-season record is the 23.0 that Myles Garrett set in 2025, breaking the 22.5 shared by
Michael Strahan (2001) and T.J. Watt (2021).[^records]

But as a way to *judge* a pass rush, sacks are a poor instrument, and the reason is simple arithmetic. A sack happens
only when three things go right for the defense: a rusher gets to the quarterback (pressure), the quarterback fails to
get rid of the ball or escape, and the rusher finishes the tackle. Only the first is mostly about the rush. So analysts
split it in two:

$$\text{sacks} = \text{pressures} \times \text{the share of pressures that become sacks}$$

[Pressure](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pressure), as Pass Protection
defined it, is any rusher forcing the quarterback to change what he wanted to do: a sack, a hit or a hurry. In FTN's
charting of the 2023–2025 regular seasons, quarterbacks were pressured on `{python} f"{100 * PR_FTN:.0f}%"` of
dropbacks and sacked on `{python} f"{100 * SR_FTN:.1f}%"`, so only about `{python} f"{100 * P2S_FTN:.0f}%"` of pressures,
roughly one in `{python} f"{1 / P2S_FTN:.0f}"`, became sacks.

Does a pressure that is *not* a sack matter? A great deal. Over the same seasons, a clean dropback was worth
`{python} f"{EPA_CLEAN:+.2f}"` expected points to the offense on average, a pressured dropback that did not end in a
sack `{python} f"{EPA_PNS:+.2f}"`, and a sack `{python} f"{EPA_SACK:+.2f}"`. Quarterbacks completed
`{python} f"{100 * CMP_CLEAN:.0f}%"` of their throws when clean and `{python} f"{100 * CMP_PNS:.0f}%"` when pressured.[^epa]
(Some of that gap is selection, since long-developing plays get pressured more often, but the direction is not in
doubt.) The hurry that nobody counts turns a good play for the offense into a slightly bad one, on many more snaps than
sacks ever do. So the question is what decides the conversion from pressure to sack, and whether it belongs to the rush
at all.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pressure-vs-sacks
#| fig-cap: "Pressure and sacks, defense by defense: every team-season from 2023 to 2025 (regular season; pressure includes sacks, from FTN's charting). Teams that pressure more do sack more, but look at the spread: at any pressure rate, sack rates differ by a factor of two. The faint rays show the conversion, the share of pressures that became sacks. The arrow follows the Cleveland Browns: in 2024 they had the highest pressure rate of any defense in these three seasons and an ordinary sack rate; in 2025 they pressured less often, converted far more of those pressures, and Myles Garrett set the single-season record. Data: nflverse play-by-play and participation via nflreadpy."
style.apply()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.4))
xs = np.linspace(100 * FTN["pr"].min() - 1.5, 100 * FTN["pr"].max() + 1.5, 10)
Y_TOP = 11.0
for k in (0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30):
    ax.plot(xs, k * xs, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
    if k * xs[-1] <= Y_TOP - 0.4:
        ax.text(xs[-1] + 0.15, k * xs[-1], f"{k:.0%} of\npressures", fontsize=6.5, color=style.MUTED,
                va="center", ha="left", linespacing=1.0)
    else:   # the ray leaves through the top of the chart: label it there
        ax.text((Y_TOP - 0.35) / k - 0.2, Y_TOP - 0.35, f"{k:.0%} of pressures", fontsize=6.5, color=style.MUTED,
                va="center", ha="right")
old, new = FTN[FTN["season"] < 2025], FTN[FTN["season"] == 2025]
ax.scatter(100 * old["pr"], 100 * old["sr"], s=18, color=style.GRID, edgecolor=style.MUTED, lw=0.4,
           label="2023-2024 defenses", zorder=2)
ax.scatter(100 * new["pr"], 100 * new["sr"], s=28, color=style.SERIES[0], edgecolor=style.SURFACE, lw=0.9,
           label="2025 defenses", zorder=3)
a, z = CLE24, CLE25
ax.annotate("", (100 * z["pr"], 100 * z["sr"]), (100 * a["pr"], 100 * a["sr"]),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=style.SERIES[1], lw=1.6, shrinkA=4, shrinkB=8), zorder=4)
ax.scatter([100 * a["pr"]], [100 * a["sr"]], s=30, color=style.SERIES[1], edgecolor=style.SURFACE, lw=0.9, zorder=4,
           label="Browns 2024 (arrow: to 2025)")
ax.annotate(f"Browns 2024\n{a['sacks']:.0f} sacks", (100 * a["pr"], 100 * a["sr"]), xytext=(-8, -16),
            textcoords="offset points", ha="right", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK)
ax.annotate(f"Browns 2025\n{z['sacks']:.0f} sacks", (100 * z["pr"], 100 * z["sr"]), xytext=(9, 6),
            textcoords="offset points", ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK)
for row, dx, dy, ha in ((DEN25, -9, 2, "right"), (SF25, 7, -4, "left")):
    ax.annotate(f"{'Broncos' if row['defteam'] == 'DEN' else '49ers'} 2025\n{row['sacks']:.0f} sacks",
                (100 * row["pr"], 100 * row["sr"]), xytext=(dx, dy), textcoords="offset points", ha=ha,
                fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK)
ax.set_xlim(xs[0], xs[-1] + 2.6)
ax.set_ylim(2, Y_TOP)
ax.set_xlabel("Pressure rate (% of opponents' dropbacks)", fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Sack rate (% of dropbacks)", fontsize=8.5)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7.4)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Three things stand out in @fig-pressure-vs-sacks.

**Pressure and sacks are related, but loosely.** Across these team-seasons the correlation between a defense's pressure
rate and its sack rate is `{python} f"{R_FTN:.2f}"`: real, but far from one. Two defenses that reach the quarterback
equally often can finish with very different sack totals. The 2025 Broncos turned
`{python} f"{100 * DEN25['p2s']:.0f}%"` of their pressures into sacks, `{python} f"{DEN25['sacks']:.0f}"` in all; the
2025 49ers turned `{python} f"{100 * SF25['p2s']:.0f}%"` into sacks and finished with
`{python} f"{SF25['sacks']:.0f}"`.

**The best pressure team was not the best sack team.** The 2024 Browns pressured opposing quarterbacks on
`{python} f"{100 * CLE24['pr']:.1f}%"` of dropbacks, the highest rate of any defense in these three seasons (far enough
from the pack that some of it may be how FTN's charters judged hurries that year; trust the ranking more than the
decimal), and finished
with `{python} f"{CLE24['sacks']:.0f}"` sacks, converting only `{python} f"{100 * CLE24['p2s']:.0f}%"`. In 2025, with
largely the same star at the heart of the rush, they pressured *less* often (`{python} f"{100 * CLE25['pr']:.1f}%"`)
and finished with `{python} f"{CLE25['sacks']:.0f}"` sacks, because `{python} f"{100 * CLE25['p2s']:.0f}%"` of their
pressures became sacks. Context shaped both years: a wide, attacking front produces many hurries that arrive just as
the ball leaves, and a team that trails often, as the 2024 Browns did, faces quarterbacks throwing quickly to catch up.
But the data that follows says the conversion itself is mostly not something a defense keeps. Garrett's record season
was real, and so was his dominance the year before; the sacks just arrived in one year rather than the other.

**So which number should you believe?** The test is which one *repeats*. A measure of skill should carry over from one
season to the next, because the players and coaches mostly carry over; a measure full of luck should not.

```{python}
#| label: fig-carryover
#| fig-cap: "What carries over from one season to the next. Each row is a correlation between a measure in one season and the same team's (or quarterback's) measure the next season; the faint dots are the individual season pairs (2018-19 to 2021-22 from Next Gen Stats' charting, 2023-24 and 2024-25 from FTN's; the 2022-23 pair is left out because the source changes), and the large dot is their average. Read the averages and the pattern, not any single dot. A defense's pressure rate repeats better than its sack rate, and even predicts next year's sacks better than this year's sacks do. A defense's pressure-to-sack conversion does not repeat at all; a quarterback's does. Data: nflverse play-by-play and participation via nflreadpy; quarterbacks with at least 100 pressured dropbacks in both seasons."
style.apply()
labels = list(CARRY)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.3))
ys = np.arange(len(labels))[::-1]
for y, k in zip(ys, labels):
    v = CARRY[k]
    ax.scatter(v, np.full(len(v), y) + np.linspace(-0.12, 0.12, len(v)), s=14, color=style.GRID,
               edgecolor=style.MUTED, lw=0.5, zorder=2)
    col = style.SERIES[1] if k.startswith("Quarterback") else style.SERIES[0]
    ax.scatter([MEAN[k]], [y], s=70, color=col, edgecolor=style.SURFACE, lw=1.0, zorder=3)
    ax.text(0.86, y, f"{MEAN[k]:+.2f}", fontsize=8, color=col, va="center", ha="left", fontweight="bold")
ax.axvline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0, zorder=1)
ax.set_yticks(ys, labels, fontsize=7.6)
ax.set_xlim(-0.3, 0.98)
ax.set_xlabel("Correlation with the next season (0 = no carry-over, 1 = perfect)", fontsize=8)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.6)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

@fig-carryover is the core of the case for pressure.[^carry] On average, a defense's pressure rate correlates about
`{python} f"{K_PR:.2f}"` with its own pressure rate the next season; its sack rate correlates only about
`{python} f"{K_SR:.2f}"` with next season's sack rate. And this season's *pressure* rate predicts next season's *sack* rate
(about `{python} f"{K_X:.2f}"`) better than this season's sack rate does. If you want to know which pass rush will get
sacks next year, count its pressures this year, not its sacks. A caution on precision: with 32 teams, any one season
pair carries a margin of roughly ±0.17, and the season pairs scatter widely. The gap between the two averages is about
two of its own standard errors, so "pressure repeats better" is solid; exactly how much better is not.

The fourth row shows why. A defense's conversion rate, the share of its pressures that become sacks, has essentially no
carry-over (an average correlation of `{python} f"{K_DP:+.2f}"`). A defense that converted a lot one year is no more likely
than any other to convert a lot the next. Whatever drives the conversion, it is not something the defense keeps.

The fifth row says what it is, or at least who. A *quarterback's* conversion rate, the share of the times he is pressured
that end in a sack, does carry over, about `{python} f"{K_QP:.2f}"` on average (noisier, because there are only twenty or
thirty quarterbacks a season with enough pressures to measure). Some quarterbacks get rid of the ball, throw it away,
step up or escape when the rush arrives, and some take the sack, year after year. How big is that? Among the
`{python} f"{Q_N}"` quarterbacks with at least 200 pressured dropbacks in 2023–2025, the conversion ran from
`{python} f"{100 * Q_LO['p2s']:.0f}%"` (`{python} Q_LO_NAME`) to `{python} f"{100 * Q_HI['p2s']:.0f}%"`
(`{python} Q_HI_NAME`), with the middle half between `{python} f"{100 * Q_25:.0f}%"` and
`{python} f"{100 * Q_75:.0f}%"`. The same rush, aimed at the quarterback at the top of that list, produces more than
twice as many sacks. FTN's charters also flag every sack they judge to be the quarterback's fault, and they
flagged about `{python} f"{100 * QB_FAULT:.0f}%"` of them, one in three.[^qbfault] [Quarterback Play](../04-the-passing-game/04-07-quarterback-play.qmd) has more
on that spread. A pass rush's sack total depends a great deal on which quarterbacks it happened to face, how often
it faced them on third-and-long, and a large helping of luck about which pressures arrived a half-step before the throw.
Pressure is the part of the sack the rush owns.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Sacks tell you who the best pass rushers are." They tell you who *finished* plays, which is real but partial. Many sacks
are **clean-up sacks**: an interior rusher collapses the pocket, the quarterback slides away from him into an edge rusher,
and the edge rusher gets the credit. Others are **coverage sacks**, where the quarterback held the ball for four or five
seconds because nobody was open, and whoever arrived first got the stat. And some of the best rushes in a game, like the
one that opened this chapter, produce a throw a beat too early and no statistic at all. Watch for who *caused* the
pressure, not just who was standing over the quarterback.
:::

## Pass rush win rate, get-off and time to pressure

If sacks are too noisy and pressure is better, can we do better still? Pressure has its own flaw: it depends on the
clock. A rusher who beats his man cleanly in 1.5 seconds against a quarterback who throws in 1.3 gets no pressure, and a
rusher who is stonewalled for four seconds and then wanders in while the quarterback pats the ball gets one. Tracking
data allows measures that do not depend on what the quarterback does.

**Pass rush win rate.** ESPN's [**pass rush win rate**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pass-rush-win-rate)
([**PRWR**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-prwr)), introduced in 2018 by ESPN Analytics and built on Next Gen Stats
tracking data, asks one question of every rush: did the rusher beat his block within 2.5 seconds of the snap?[^prwr] Its
companion, pass block win rate, asks the reverse of every blocker. The fixed 2.5-second clock is the clever part. It
sits a little before the average throw, ESPN found it best separated the rushers and blockers already known to be good, and it takes the quarterback out of the number: a quarterback who holds
the ball cannot hand rushers late "wins," and one who throws quickly cannot hide a rusher who was about to get home.
ESPN publishes it as leaderboards ranked within position groups, so edge rushers are compared with edge rushers and
interior linemen with interior linemen, because their jobs are so different. For a scale: when ESPN introduced it, four
weeks into the 2018 season, the average edge rusher won about 22% of his rushes and the leaders were in the 40s. A
rusher who wins one rush in three is very good; one in five is ordinary. Double teams get special care: since 2019,
beating one blocker of a double team no longer counts as a win, which is why an interior rusher who wins often against
constant doubles is so impressive.

Its limits are worth knowing. A "win" is not a pressure; a rusher can beat his man and still be too late or too wide to
matter. A bull rush that walks the tackle into the quarterback without ever shedding him is the kind of rep a
"did he beat his block" measure can miss. The model does not know each rusher's assignment, so a penetrator on a stunt, whose job is to occupy blockers,
can look like a loser while doing exactly what was asked. And the play-by-play data is not public, only the leaderboards,
so you cannot rebuild it yourself. Use it the way you would use a scout's opinion: an excellent tiebreaker between
players, not a final verdict.

**Get-off and time to pressure.** Two simpler tracking measures bracket the rush. Get-off, as above, is how quickly a
rusher crosses the line after the snap. **Time to pressure** is the seconds from the snap to the first pressure on the
play. Together they separate the rushes that won from the ones that were handed something. A pressure inside about two and
a half seconds, before most throws are due, is almost always a rush win. One after three and a half seconds, when
every route has finished, is usually the coverage, the quarterback holding the ball, or both. In between is shared
credit: the routes are just finishing, and the rush and coverage are working together. Here is how each is computed
from tracking data, on a simulated four-man rush.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ttp-strip
#| fig-cap: "A four-man rush measured from tracking data (simulated, BDB-format; receivers and coverage not shown). 1: the snap. 2: under a second later all four rushers have crossed the line; each one's get-off is the frame he crossed it. 3: the right end gets past the right tackle (deeper than him, toward the quarterback): his rush is won, well inside the 2.5-second window pass rush win rate uses. 4: the end reaches two yards of the quarterback, this chapter's working definition of pressure for the measurement, and the quarterback has to move. The other three rushers are still in front of their blockers."
def measured_rush():
    """A four-man rush against five blockers: the right end wins with speed, the others are held up."""
    p = Play(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q")], four_down(), los=35, to_go=None)
    timed(p, "QB", [(0.9, -7.0, 0.0), (2.1, -7.0, 0.0), (2.8, -6.4, -1.4)])
    timed(p, "RE", [(0.1, 1.0, 5.4), (0.5, 0.0, 5.8), (0.95, -1.9, 6.2), (1.3, -3.2, 5.8), (1.7, -4.5, 4.7),
                    (2.0, -5.6, 3.0), (2.3, -6.3, 1.6), (2.8, -6.5, 0.1)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RT", [(0.4, -1.4, 3.7), (0.8, -2.2, 4.2), (1.2, -2.8, 4.3), (1.6, -3.2, 4.1), (2.0, -3.5, 3.9),
                    (2.8, -3.8, 3.6)], "block")
    timed(p, "LE", [(0.35, 1.0, -5.4), (0.8, 0.0, -5.8), (1.2, -1.3, -6.0), (1.8, -2.4, -5.6), (2.4, -3.0, -5.1),
                    (2.8, -3.2, -4.8)], "rush")
    timed(p, "LT", [(0.4, -1.4, -3.7), (0.9, -2.3, -4.4), (1.4, -3.0, -4.6), (2.0, -3.6, -4.2), (2.8, -3.9, -3.5)],
          "block")
    timed(p, "NT", [(0.25, 1.0, -0.7), (0.7, 0.0, -0.75), (1.2, -0.8, -0.8), (2.0, -1.25, -0.8), (2.8, -1.5, -0.8)],
          "rush")
    timed(p, "C", [(0.4, -1.3, -0.1), (1.0, -1.9, -0.2), (2.0, -2.3, -0.2), (2.8, -2.6, -0.2)], "block")
    timed(p, "LG", [(0.4, -1.2, -1.8), (1.0, -1.6, -1.6), (2.0, -2.1, -1.6), (2.8, -2.4, -1.6)], "block")
    timed(p, "DT", [(0.1, 1.0, 2.35), (0.5, 0.0, 2.3), (1.2, -0.9, 2.1), (2.0, -1.35, 2.0), (2.8, -1.7, 1.9)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RG", [(0.4, -1.3, 1.8), (1.2, -2.0, 1.9), (2.0, -2.3, 1.9), (2.8, -2.8, 1.9)], "block")
    return p


MR = measured_rush()
TRK = MR.to_tracking()               # simulated tracking in Big Data Bowl columns: frameId, time, x, y, ...
LOS_X = MR.los
RUSHERS = {"LE": "left end", "NT": "1-technique", "DT": "3-technique", "RE": "right end"}
frames = TRK[TRK["time"] >= 0]
qb = frames[frames["displayName"] == "QB"].set_index("time")[["x", "y"]]
GETOFF, DIST = {}, {}
for k in RUSHERS:
    r = frames[frames["displayName"] == k].set_index("time")[["x", "y"]]
    GETOFF[k] = float(r.index[r["x"] <= LOS_X + 1e-9][0])          # first frame on or past the line
    DIST[k] = np.hypot(r["x"] - qb["x"], r["y"] - qb["y"])
near = pd.concat(DIST, axis=1).min(axis=1)
TTP = float(near.index[near <= 2.0][0])                              # first frame within 2 yards of the QB
rt = frames[frames["displayName"] == "RT"].set_index("time")["x"]
re_ = frames[frames["displayName"] == "RE"].set_index("time")["x"]
WIN_T = float(re_.index[(re_ < rt - 0.5)][0])                        # the end half a yard deeper than his blocker
ALL_ACROSS = float(np.ceil(max(GETOFF.values()) * 10) / 10) + 0.3   # a beat after the last one crossed
strip(MR, [0.0, ALL_ACROSS, WIN_T, TTP],
      notes=["snap", "all four have crossed the line:\neach one's get-off is logged",
             f"+{WIN_T:.1f} s: the end gets past\nthe tackle: a rush 'win'",
             f"+{TTP:.1f} s: within 2 yards\nof the QB: pressure"],
      lateral=(-8.0, 8.0), window=(-9.4, 2.6), ncols=2, rings=(("RE", style.THIRD),))
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-ttp-chart
#| fig-cap: "The same simulated rush as numbers: each rusher's distance from the quarterback, frame by frame (ten per second). For the first half-second or so the distances rise or hold steady, because the quarterback is dropping back as fast as the rushers are closing. The dots mark each rusher's get-off, the frame he crossed the line. The dashed horizontal line is the two-yard pressure threshold used here; the right end crosses it first, which is the play's time to pressure. The shaded band is pass rush win rate's 2.5-second window: the end beat his blocker inside it, so his rush counts as a win, while the other three never beat theirs."
style.apply()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.9))
END_Y = {}
for k, name in RUSHERS.items():
    col = style.SERIES[1] if k == "RE" else style.MUTED
    d = DIST[k][DIST[k].index <= 2.8]
    ax.plot(d.index, d.values, color=col, lw=2.2 if k == "RE" else 1.3, zorder=3)
    ax.plot([GETOFF[k]], [float(DIST[k].loc[GETOFF[k]])], "o", ms=5, color=col, mec="white", mew=0.7, zorder=4)
    END_Y[k] = float(d.values[-1])
ys_lab, last = {}, None
for k in sorted(END_Y, key=END_Y.get):            # spread the end labels so none overlap
    y = END_Y[k] if last is None else max(END_Y[k], last + 0.62)
    ys_lab[k], last = y, y
for k, name in RUSHERS.items():
    ax.text(2.84, ys_lab[k], name, fontsize=7.2, color=style.SERIES[1] if k == "RE" else style.INK_2, va="center")
ax.axhline(2.0, color=style.SERIES[7], lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=2)
ax.text(0.05, 2.25, "pressure: within 2 yards", fontsize=7, color=style.SERIES[7], va="bottom")
ax.axvspan(0, 2.5, color=style.SERIES[0], alpha=0.06, zorder=0)
ax.text(1.25, 9.6, "pass rush win rate's 2.5-second window", fontsize=7,
        color=style.SERIES[0], ha="center", va="top")
ax.axvline(TTP, color=style.SERIES[1], lw=1.0, ls=(0, (1, 1.5)), zorder=2)
ax.text(TTP - 0.05, 8.3, f"time to pressure\n{TTP:.1f} s", fontsize=7, color=style.SERIES[1], ha="right", va="center")
ax.set_xlim(0, 3.45)
ax.set_ylim(0, 10)
ax.set_xlabel("seconds after the snap", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("yards to the QB", fontsize=8)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.6)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

In this simulated play the rushers' get-offs range from `{python} f"{min(GETOFF.values()):.1f}"` to
`{python} f"{max(GETOFF.values()):.1f}"` seconds, the right end beats his tackle at `{python} f"{WIN_T:.1f}"` seconds, and
the time to pressure is `{python} f"{TTP:.1f}"` seconds, inside two and a half: a rush win by the stopwatch too. On a
real play the definitions need more care than a two-yard
circle (data providers use their own rules for what counts as pressure, and real players are not points), but the logic
is exactly this, and it is the logic you will build on real Big Data Bowl frames in
[Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl](../13-analytics-and-data/13-05-tracking-data-and-big-data-bowl.qmd).

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (the same measurements on a real Big Data Bowl play)"
# Run this after downloading a Big Data Bowl edition (see 13-05). Column names differ by year;
# gridiron.bdb.prepare() normalizes direction (offense moving +x) and labels each player 'off', 'def' or 'ball'.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb

trk_all = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_1.csv")
plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
players = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/players.csv")[["nflId", "position"]]
one = bdb.prepare(trk_all, plays, game_id=2022091100, play_id=55).merge(players, on="nflId", how="left")
after = one[one["time"] >= 0]
los_x = float(one.loc[(one["time"] == 0) & (one["side"] == "ball"), "x"].iloc[0])
qb = after[after["position"] == "QB"].set_index("time")[["x", "y"]]
rushers = after[(after["side"] == "def") & after["position"].isin(["DE", "DT", "NT", "OLB"])]
for nfl_id, r in rushers.groupby("nflId"):
    r = r.set_index("time")
    crossed = r.index[r["x"] <= los_x]                      # get-off: first frame on or past the line
    dist = np.hypot(r["x"] - qb["x"], r["y"] - qb["y"])     # distance to the passer, frame by frame
    close = dist.index[dist <= 2.0]                         # a simple pressure rule; providers use their own
    print(r["displayName"].iloc[0], "get-off", crossed.min() if len(crossed) else None,
          "within 2 yd at", close.min() if len(close) else None)
```

## Where the moves came from

The modern pass rusher's ancestor is Deacon Jones, the Los Angeles Rams' defensive end of the 1960s, a ferocious
speed rusher who is credited with coining the word "sack" for what he did to quarterbacks. His signature weapon was the
**head slap**: a blow to the side of the blocker's helmet at the snap to stun him for an instant, then go around him. The
NFL banned the head slap in 1977, and blows to the head have been illegal for rushers ever since.[^deacon] A year later
the 1978 rule changes went the other way for blockers, letting them extend their arms and open their hands on pass
blocks ([The 1978 Liberation](../11-history/11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd) tells that story). Together, the two changes turned the
pass rush into what it is now: a fight between the rusher's hands and the blocker's, aimed at arms and chests, where
technique and timing matter as much as violence.

Then came the player who made offenses rebuild their protections around him: Lawrence Taylor, the Giants' outside
linebacker from 1981, rushing from a two-point stance on the edge of a 3-4 with a speed no blocker of the time could
match (Pass Protection told how offenses answered him with extra blockers). In 1986 he had 20.5 sacks and was the
league's Most Valuable Player, the last defensive player to win the award,[^lt] and the value of the left tackle, who
blocks a right-handed quarterback's blind side, rose with him. Defenses still like a great rusher on that side,
but many of today's best flip sides from week to week, or snap to snap, to hunt whichever tackle is weaker.

Reggie White, "the Minister of Defense," showed what power and hands could do. After fifteen seasons, most of them
with the Eagles and the Packers, he retired as the NFL's career sack leader, with 198 (Bruce Smith later passed him, finishing with 200), and his
signature, the "hump" move, was a club-and-lift: a forearm club up under the blocker's arm that lifted and threw him
aside, a rip and a bull rush in one violent motion.[^white] In the 2000s Dwight Freeney's spin move made a smaller, quicker body type
dangerous on the edge. And in the 2010s Aaron Donald proved that the most dangerous rusher on the field could line up
inside.

Today's edge rushers study tackles' sets on film like quarterbacks study coverages, and the hand fight has become its
own discipline: the long arm, the cross-chop, the ghost. T.J. Watt tied the sack record in 2021 and won Defensive
Player of the Year; Myles Garrett broke it in 2025 and won the award unanimously.[^dpoy] And Micah Parsons, the
Cowboys' first-round pick in 2021, made a different point: drafted as an off-ball linebacker, he became one of the
league's most feared rushers by lining up all over the front, over a guard one snap and wide on the edge the next, so
that protections could never be sure where to slide. Dallas traded him to Green Bay just before the 2025 season, for two first-round picks and defensive tackle Kenny
Clark.[^parsons]

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Cleveland Browns 2025 — Myles Garrett's record"}
**The play to find.** Week 18 of 2025, the Browns at Cincinnati, fourth quarter, `{python} G_CLOCK` left: Garrett
sacks `{python} G_QB.replace("J.", "Joe ")` for his 23rd sack of the season, the one that broke the record.[^gsack]
He was playing in Jim Schwartz's attacking front (Schwartz was the Browns' defensive coordinator from 2023 to 2025),
which lines its ends up wide and sends them upfield.[^schwartz]

**What to notice:** then pick any Browns passing down from that season and watch only Garrett and the man blocking him.

- **The alignment.** Which side is he on, and how wide? Wide means a long arc and a running start.
- **The get-off.** Count how often he is the first player on the field to move, and where he meets the tackle: in
  front of him, or level with him at the corner.
- **The first move, then the second.** Note what he shows in the first quarter and what he does in the fourth. Look
  for the speed-to-power: three steps of speed, then straight into the tackle's chest.
- **The help, and his answer.** Count how often the offense chips him with a back or tight end or slides its
  protection toward him, and watch how he beats the chip: by rushing through the chipper's outside shoulder, or by
  starting wider so the back cannot reach him. Every extra man on Garrett is a one-on-one for someone else.
- **The finish.** On his sacks, notice how many came quickly (a rush win) and how many came after the quarterback
  had held the ball (a coverage or clean-up sack).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Super Bowls LIX and LX — pressure with four"}
**The games.** The last two Super Bowls were won by defenses that got to the quarterback without blitzing. In Super
Bowl LIX (February 2025) the Eagles rushed four or fewer on `{python} f"{LIX['four']}"` of Patrick Mahomes's
`{python} f"{LIX['db']}"` dropbacks and sacked him `{python} f"{LIX['sacks']}"` times, `{python} f"{LIX['sacks4']}"` of
them with four or fewer rushers. In Super Bowl LX (February 2026) the Seahawks rushed four or fewer on
`{python} f"{LX['four']}"` of Drake Maye's `{python} f"{LX['db']}"` dropbacks and sacked him `{python} f"{LX['sacks']}"`
times, `{python} f"{LX['sacks4']}"` of them with four or fewer.[^sb] Mike Macdonald's Seattle defense has a reputation
for four-man *simulated pressures*, in which a lineman drops and a linebacker or defensive back rushes in his place
([Zone Blitzes and Simulated Pressure](07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd) shows how). Macdonald himself
pushed back on that in November 2025 ("We do not run a lot of simulated pressures"),[^mac] and the Super Bowl bears him
out: FTN's charters counted a blitzer on only `{python} f"{LX_SIM}"` of Seattle's `{python} f"{LX_FOUR_FTN}"`
four-man rushes. Mostly, its four were its front four, winning.

**What to notice:**

- **Count the rushers on every dropback.** Almost always four. Then count the coverage behind them: seven men for at
  most five receivers.
- **Look for the stunts.** On long downs, watch for two rushers crossing paths, and ask which blocker the looper was
  aimed at.
- **Time the pressure.** Count from the snap to the moment the quarterback has to move, and see how many pressures
  arrive before the receivers have finished their routes.

The Eagles' game is studied in [the Eagles case study](../12-case-studies/12-06-eagles-trenches-and-tush-push.qmd),
and Seattle's defense, built by Mike Macdonald, in
[Fangio's Two-High Revolution and Macdonald's Answer](../12-case-studies/12-08-two-high-to-macdonald.qmd).
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**Before the snap.**

- **Find the best rusher and his alignment.** Wide outside the tackle (built for speed), tight over him (power and
  inside moves), or standing up over a guard (he is being moved around to beat the protection).
- **Count the rushers you expect and the blockers you see.** Four rushers against five or six blockers means the
  defense is trusting its four; look at the coverage behind them.
- **Check the down and distance.** Third-and-long is when stunts and patient rushes have time to work; on
  third-and-2 the ball will be out too fast for either.
- **Is the quarterback a runner?** If so, expect the ends to rush with discipline, and maybe a spy.
- **Where is the help?** Find the back and any tight end. One aligned near the best rusher probably means a chip, and
  at the snap the linemen's first steps tell you slide or man (all five stepping the same way is a slide). Stunts and
  the best rusher's moves are aimed away from the help.

**After the snap: the stopwatch drill.**

- **Count the seconds** from the snap to the first pressure ("one-Mississippi"), or use a stopwatch on a replay.
  Under about two and a half seconds is a rush win. Past three and a half, the coverage or the quarterback owns most
  of it. In between, they share it.
- **Note whether the ball was already out.** A rusher who arrives just after the throw has still done his job if he
  made the quarterback throw early; a rusher who arrives after a five-second hold was handed it.
- **Name the move.** Around the corner (speed and rip), through the chest (bull or long arm), or back inside
  (swim, spin). In the fourth quarter, look for the counter to whatever worked in the first.
- **Watch for crossing paths.** Two rushers swapping lanes is a stunt; find the looper, and see which blocker he
  was aimed at, and whether the blockers passed it off.
- **Check the lanes.** If the quarterback escapes, freeze the replay and find the rusher who left his lane.

**For your prediction log:** for one quarter, write down on every dropback the number of rushers, your stopwatch time
to pressure (or "none"), and whether the ball was out first. You will see which defenses win early and which only win
late.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: third-and-long against five"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-stunt
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-11. The offense is in an empty formation, three receivers right and two left, so only the five linemen can block. The defense shows four linemen (a 1-technique shaded to the center's left, a 3-technique to the right, an end outside each tackle), two linebackers walked out over the slot receivers, and two deep safeties. The two defenders on the right side of the line are ringed."
def quiet_line():
    """The five linemen with only the center labelled: on full-width drills the two-letter labels overprint."""
    return [q.moved(label="C" if q.key == "C" else "") for q in line()]


def empty_3x2():
    return quiet_line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0), O("A", "WR", -1.4, -9.5),
                     O("Y", "TE", -1.4, 6.5), O("H", "WR", -1.4, 10.5), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 15.0)]


dfn = four_down() + [D("WILL", "WILL", 5.0, -6.0, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.8, 4.6, "M"),
                     D("NB", "NB", 5.0, 10.0, "NB"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -15.0, "CB"),
                     D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 15.0, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -7.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 13.0, 7.0, "SS")]
p = Play(empty_3x2(), dfn, los=40, to_go=11)
p.highlight("DT", "RE", color=PURPLE)
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.4, lateral=(-17.0, 17.0), window=(-7.0, 14.6))
plt.show()
```

**Is this a good down for a stunt? If so, which one, aimed where, and what is the defense risking?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Yes: this is the down stunts are made for, and a T-E on the right, with the 3-technique picking the right tackle
and the end looping inside, is the natural call.** *The clock:* on third-and-11 the quarterback needs routes that get
past the line to gain, so he will usually hold the ball two and a half seconds or more, long enough for a looper to
arrive. *The numbers:* five blockers against four rushers gives the offense one spare man, but against this front the
spare is the left guard, uncovered on the far side. Aim the stunt at the right guard and right tackle, away from him,
and those two must pass it off alone. *The choice:* T-E rather than E-T if the end is the better rusher, because the
looper is the man who arrives free.

Two cautions. If the offense slides its five-man protection toward that side, the center, right guard and right
tackle all step that way and own those gaps, and the stunt is absorbed. You cannot see that from the pre-snap picture,
which is why defenses study how a team protects from empty before calling it. And the stunt moves the right side's
contain from the end to the 3-technique: against a quarterback who runs, a washed-out 3-technique turns third-and-11
into a scramble. Against a pocket passer, most defenses happily take that risk.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: the quarterback who runs"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-mush
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-6. The offense is in the shotgun with three wide receivers, a tight end, and a back beside a quarterback (ringed in green) who is one of the league's most dangerous runners. The defense is in a nickel with four linemen, including a wide-9 end (w9) on the right."
off = quiet_line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -2.0, "R"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0),
                      O("H", "WR", -1.4, -9.5), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8), O("Z", "WR", -1.4, 15.0)]
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -5.4, "E"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "1"), D("DT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "3"),
       D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 7.1, "w9"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, 1.3, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, -3.0, "W"),
       D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -9.0, "NB"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.4, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.4, 15.0, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -6.5, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 6.5, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=6)
p.highlight("QB")
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.4, lateral=(-17.0, 17.0), window=(-7.0, 14.6))
plt.show()
```

**How do you expect the four to rush, which of them has the hardest job, and what is the defense giving up?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Expect a mush rush.** On third-and-6, a quarterback who runs does not need a receiver to get open; he needs one
lane. So the defense's first priority is that no lane opens, and its second is the sack.

**The wide-9 end has the hardest job**, because his alignment is built for the long, fast arc that runs an end past
the quarterback and opens the escape lane in @fig-rush-lanes, on the quarterback's throwing-arm side at that. Expect
him to tighten his alignment before the snap, or, if he stays wide, to rush through the tackle's outside half rather
than around him. The other side is less of a worry: the back, lined up on the quarterback's left, will likely chip
the left end or stay in to block, and the tight end beside the right tackle can chip the wide-9 on his way out, which
is one more reason that end cannot win with speed alone. Expect fewer stunts, and don't be surprised if a linebacker
mirrors the quarterback instead of covering anyone: a spy.

**The price is time**: the coverage, with six or seven men, must hold for four seconds or more, and if anyone breaks
contain, the play you will see is the one the defense feared most, a quarterback through the hole and past the line
to gain.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: the counter"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-counter
#| fig-cap: "Fourth quarter. The defense's best rusher (E) has beaten this right tackle *inside* twice today with a spin, once for a sack. On this snap the tackle has set short and square, sitting inside, determined not to be spun again; the right guard has the 3-technique in front of him. The picture is about 0.8 seconds after the snap: the faint square is where the rusher is now, early in his arc."
p = Play(line(["RG", "RT"]), [D("DT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "3"), D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4, "E")], los=35, to_go=None)
to(p, "RT", (-1.2, 3.7))
to(p, "RG", (-1.5, 1.8))
to(p, "DT", (-0.4, 2.2), "rush")
to(p, "RE", (-0.9, 6.6), "rush", via=[(0.2, 6.2)])
fld = draw(p, width_in=5.0, lateral=(-0.8, 10.6), window=(-7.2, 3.4))
ghost(fld, p, -0.9, 6.6, "E")
point_to(fld, p, (-3.6, 6.6), (-1.2, 3.7), "the tackle sets short\nand square, sitting inside", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
say(fld, p, -5.6, 1.4, "QB this way", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.6)
plt.show()
```

**What move is coming, and what can the offense do about it, this snap and the next?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The speed rush, around the corner: a dip and rip.** This is the rush plan paying off from the other direction. Twice
the rusher won inside, so the tackle has stopped bailing: he is sitting short and square to protect the inside. But a
tackle who has not gained depth has no time to get back to the corner, and the rusher meets him level before he can
turn and run. The spin is
the wrong answer now; that is exactly the move the tackle is sitting on.

The offense has fewer answers on this snap than you might think. The right guard cannot help outside, because the
3-technique is on him. The quarterback's best move is to step up into the pocket, so the rusher's arc carries him past
behind. **Next snaps:** the tackle varies his sets (a [jump set](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-jump-set) at the line,
or a [45-degree set](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd) instead of sitting) so the rusher cannot read
the set and pick the counter; the offense chips the rusher with a back or tight end on the way out; and the play caller
calls quick throws, so the ball is gone before any move can finish. That is the conversation across a game in
miniature: the rusher made the tackle afraid of one thing, and now the offense has to change the question.
:::
:::

## Back to the replay

Return to the play that opened the chapter. Third-and-8, four rushers, an end who took three strides up the arc and
then drove straight into the tackle: **speed-to-power**, set up by every speed rush he had shown before. The tackle,
fearing the corner, had kicked back fast, so his weight was going backward when the end turned into him, and he could
not anchor. The pocket collapsed from the side, the quarterback threw early, and the pass sailed.

The box score has nothing for the end. FTN's charters would mark that dropback as pressured. Pass rush win rate might well
count it as a win, though a bull rush that never sheds the blocker is the kind of rep a beat-the-block measure can
miss. And a stopwatch would put the pressure at
about two seconds, early enough that it was entirely the rush's doing. That is the whole chapter in one snap: the
moves, the plan that set them up, and the reason a coach values the hurry that nobody counts more than the sack total
everybody does.

## Takeaways

- **The rush is a race and a fight.** A rusher must beat a bigger blocker before the ball is out, a little under three
  seconds on average. Get-off decides where they meet: a tenth of a second is most of a yard, and meeting the tackle
  level at the corner instead of in front of him is the difference between winning and losing.
- **Each move punishes a mistake.** Speed beats a slow set; the bull rush and long arm beat a high, light or retreating
  one; the swim, rip and spin beat a blocker who has committed. Cross-chops and ghosts beat the punch itself.
- **The best rushers have a plan.** They show one move until the tackle adjusts, then use the counter his adjustment
  opens; speed-to-power works *because* tackles fear speed.
- **Stunts win with geometry.** T-E, E-T and interior twists exchange rushers to beat man blocking or choose matchups
  against slides, at the cost of time and of lanes.
- **Four rush lanes make a box.** Ends keep contain, the middle pushes the pocket; against a quarterback who runs,
  the mush rush squeezes instead of racing and accepts a longer clock.
- **Count pressure, not sacks.** Pressure carries over from season to season and predicts future sacks; the share of
  pressures that become sacks mostly does not, except as a trait of the quarterback. Pass rush win rate, get-off and
  time to pressure use tracking data to take the quarterback out of the measure.

[Defensive Line Play](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd) (technique
numbers, one-gap penetration, the wide-9 and contain). The quarterback's share of sacks comes from

**Sets up:** [Blitzing](07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd), where the defense stops trying to win with four and adds
